CMPCT-005.description:
Replace the current LLM-based batch anchor detection and narrative summary compaction with a three-layer architecture that uses in-view DAG construction.

Key insight: instead of running compaction in a background process with separate LLM calls, the agent itself builds the hierarchical summary DAG in the same conversation view using /clear + SessionSearch + a new inject_summary tool. The agent IS the summarizer — zero marginal LLM cost.

Verified: /clear only clears in-memory state (messages, turns, token_tracker). It never touches the on-disk persistence layer. All pre-clear messages remain fully searchable via SessionSearch (which reads from the JSONL message store, not in-memory state).

Layer 0 — Structurally Lossless Trimming: Before DAG construction, deterministically strip mechanical bloat from SessionSearch results (raw tool outputs replaced with condensed references, file contents from Read replaced with path references, base64 data stripped, verbose Edit parameters collapsed). Zero LLM cost, fully reversible from persisted originals. CMV (Santoni 2026) shows 20-86% token reduction from this alone. Trimming is applied automatically during DAG construction only via an implicit compaction_in_progress flag on BackgroundSession.

Layer 1 — In-View DAG Construction: When compaction triggers, the flow is: (1) /clear (context emptied, persistence intact), (2) agent retrieves previous history via targeted SessionSearch calls (with Layer 0 trimming applied to results), (3) agent writes hierarchical DAG summary with D0 (detailed: files, decisions, errors), D1 (arc-level: attempts, outcomes), D2 (durable: architecture, milestones) depth levels, each with turn range references for future SessionSearch drilldown, (4) agent calls inject_summary to pin the DAG and drop all builder turns. The agent has full judgment over what to keep — it knows which decisions are still in effect, which explorations were dead ends, and what the current work state is.

Layer 2 — Emergency Threshold Compaction: Existing threshold trigger as safety net. Auto-triggers /clear and instructs the agent to build its DAG via SessionSearch. Never drops below system reminders + injected DAG + last user message.

New tool required: inject_summary(content) — pins DAG content as system-level message (wrapped in <system-reminder type=compaction-dag>), drops all builder turns using the same partition_for_compaction() → clear → restore pattern as execute_compaction(), returns injected token count and remaining budget. Builder turns remain on disk (persisted during streaming) and are recoverable via SessionSearch.

This replaces the current expensive batch system (2 large LLM calls per compaction, 50k+ tokens) with zero-marginal-cost agent-driven summarization. Inspired by CMV, LCM, Focus, ACON, HiAgent, SimpleMem, H-MEM research (see attachments).

CMPCT-006.description:
Create `codelet/core/src/compaction/trimmer.rs` — a deterministic, zero-LLM-cost content transformer that strips mechanical bloat from StoredMessage content before the agent sees it during DAG construction.

## Research Foundation

This implements the core insight from CMV (Santoni, Imperial College London, arXiv:2602.22402, Feb 2026): the highest-ROI intervention for context management is stripping raw tool outputs BEFORE any lossy compression. CMV demonstrates 20% mean token reduction (up to 86% for tool-heavy sessions) from structurally lossless trimming alone — preserving every user message and assistant reasoning verbatim while replacing verbose tool parameters/results with compact references.

The Deep Agents SDK (LangChain) validates the same principle: structured tool output replacement is economically viable even under prompt caching, with break-even within 10 turns for mixed tool-use sessions (39% average reduction per CMV).

## What To Build

A `Trimmer` struct with a `trim_message(stored_msg: &StoredMessage) -> String` method that applies deterministic transformation rules:

| Content Type | Trim Action | Replacement |
|---|---|---|
| Read tool results (file content) | Replace with reference | `[file: {path}, {lines} lines, {tokens} tok — use Read to retrieve]` |
| Write tool parameters (full content) | Replace with reference | `[Write: {path}, {lines} lines — file persisted to disk]` |
| Edit tool parameters (old_string/new_string) | Condense | `[Edit: {path} — replaced {old_len} chars with {new_len} chars]` |
| Bash tool output (stdout/stderr) | Truncate head+tail | First 10 lines + `... ({N} lines omitted)` + last 5 lines + exit code |
| Base64 image data | Strip entirely | `[image: {W}x{H}, {bytes} bytes, from {path}]` |
| Search/Grep tool output | Truncate matches | First 10 matches + `... ({N} more matches)` |

**Key constraint:** Trimming NEVER touches user messages or assistant reasoning text. Only structured tool parameters and tool result outputs are transformed.

## Codebase Integration Points

- **Input type:** `StoredMessage` from `codelet/napi/src/persistence/` — has `role: String`, `content: String`, and `metadata: HashMap<String, Value>`. The metadata field contains tool information (tool name, input parameters) serialized from `AssistantContent::ToolUse`.
- **Output:** Transformed content `String` — the trimmed version of `stored_msg.content`.
- **Caller:** Will be invoked from `session_search_handler.rs` (see CMPCT-010) via `resolve_message_content()` when the `compaction_in_progress` flag is set.
- **Re-export:** Add `pub mod trimmer;` and `pub use trimmer::Trimmer;` to `codelet/core/src/compaction/mod.rs`.

## Files To Create

- `codelet/core/src/compaction/trimmer.rs` — Trimmer struct and all transformation rules
- `codelet/core/src/compaction/__tests__/trimmer.test.rs` — Comprehensive tests

## Files To Modify

- `codelet/core/src/compaction/mod.rs` — Add module declaration and re-export

## Acceptance Criteria

- Each trimming rule from the table has a dedicated unit test
- User messages pass through completely unchanged
- Assistant reasoning text passes through completely unchanged
- Messages without tool metadata pass through unchanged
- Token count of trimmed output is measurably smaller than input
- All trimming is fully reversible by re-reading the persisted originals via SessionSearch

CMPCT-007.description:
Extend `codelet/core/src/compaction/model.rs` with a `StructuralAnnotation` enum for per-turn inline signal detection. These annotations provide zero-cost metadata that the agent can reference during DAG construction to identify important turns without reading full content.

## Research Foundation

This preserves the correct insight from CMPCT-004 (per-turn structural signal detection) while reframing it as metadata rather than content. ACON (Kang et al., KAIST/Microsoft, arXiv:2510.00615, Oct 2025) demonstrates that preserving WHY decisions were made — not just WHAT tool was called — is critical for continuation quality. The annotations capture structural milestones (fspec status changes, error resolutions, file modifications) that the agent can use as navigation aids during SessionSearch retrieval.

HiAgent (Hu et al., ACL 2025, aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.1575) validates that agent-controlled compression boundaries based on structural signals (subgoal completions) produce better results than external heuristics. Our annotations provide these structural signals.

## What To Build

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum StructuralAnnotation {
    /// fspec milestone reached (from Fspec tool call with specific command)
    FspecMilestone {
        command: String,     // e.g., "update-work-unit-status"
        args: Vec<String>,   // e.g., ["AUTH-001", "implementing"]
    },
    /// Error was resolved (previous failure + current file modification + all-success)
    ErrorResolution {
        failed_tool: String,
        resolved_file: String,
    },
    /// File modification (from Edit/Write tool calls)
    FileModification {
        path: String,
        operation: FileOp, // Created, Modified, Deleted
    },
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub enum FileOp {
    Created,
    Modified,
    Deleted,
}
```

## Codebase Integration Points

- **Location:** `codelet/core/src/compaction/model.rs` — alongside existing `ConversationTurn`, `ToolCall`, `ToolResult`
- **Deprecations:** `PreservationContext` and `BuildStatus` (currently at lines 220+ of model.rs) become `#[deprecated]` — subsumed by agent judgment during DAG construction. These contain flaky heuristics like `detect_build_status()` matching substrings "pass"/"fail" against arbitrary tool output.
- **Kept unchanged:** `TokenTracker` — tracks API-level token usage, orthogonal to compaction strategy.
- **Re-export:** Update `codelet/core/src/compaction/mod.rs` to export `StructuralAnnotation` and `FileOp`.
- **Consumer:** The per-turn annotation detector (CMPCT-011) will attach these to persisted messages during the stream loop. The agent sees them via SessionSearch metadata during DAG construction.

## Files To Modify

- `codelet/core/src/compaction/model.rs` — Add StructuralAnnotation enum, FileOp enum, deprecate PreservationContext/BuildStatus
- `codelet/core/src/compaction/mod.rs` — Update re-exports

## Acceptance Criteria

- StructuralAnnotation enum is serializable/deserializable (round-trip test)
- FileOp enum covers Created, Modified, Deleted
- PreservationContext and BuildStatus marked #[deprecated]
- All existing tests still compile (deprecated items still usable with warnings)
- TokenTracker remains unchanged

CMPCT-008.description:
Create `codelet/tools/src/inject_summary.rs` — the Rig Tool definition for `inject_summary`, following the same handler-dispatch pattern used by `SessionSearchTool` (codelet/tools/src/session_search/) and `FspecTool` (codelet/tools/src/fspec.rs).

## Research Foundation

This tool is the mechanism through which the agent completes its self-directed compression cycle. Focus (Verma, arXiv:2601.07190, Jan 2026) demonstrated that agents with explicit compression primitives (`start_focus`/`complete_focus`) achieve 22.7% token reduction with zero accuracy loss. Our `inject_summary` is the single completion primitive — the agent calls it after building its DAG to pin the summary and discard builder turns.

LCM (Ehrlich & Blackman, Voltropy PBC, Feb 2026) provides DAG navigation tools (`lcm_describe`, `lcm_grep`, `lcm_expand_query`). In our design, `inject_summary` replaces the need for these — the agent writes the entire hierarchical DAG itself and pins it via this tool, while SessionSearch handles all retrieval.

## What To Build

A tool struct implementing the Rig `Tool` trait with:

```rust
Tool name: "inject_summary"
Tool description: "Pin a hierarchical DAG summary as system-level content, dropping all builder turns from the active context. Call this after building your session summary via SessionSearch. The content is wrapped as a system-reminder (type: compaction-dag) and persisted across future compactions."

Parameters:
  content: String (required) — The DAG summary content to inject

Return:
  injected_tokens: u64 — Token count of the injected DAG
  remaining_budget: u64 — Available context budget after injection
```

## Handler Pattern (from codebase)

The tool does NOT perform the session manipulation directly. Following the pattern established by `SessionSearchTool` and `FspecTool`:

1. Tool definition and JSON schema live in `codelet-tools` crate
2. A handler type alias is defined: `pub type InjectSummaryHandler = Arc<dyn Fn(String) -> InjectSummaryResult + Send + Sync>;`
3. A global handler registry (like `set_session_search_handler()` in `codelet/tools/src/lib.rs` at line ~112) stores per-session handlers
4. The actual session manipulation code lives in the NAPI handler (CMPCT-009)
5. When `call()` is invoked, the tool dispatches to the registered handler

See `codelet/tools/src/fspec.rs` for the cleanest example of this pattern: `FspecTool` defines the schema, `set_fspec_handler_for_session()` manages the registry, and the actual logic is in `codelet/napi/src/fspec.rs`.

See `codelet/tools/src/session_search/mod.rs` for the SessionSearch equivalent: `SessionSearchTool` defines the schema, `set_session_search_handler()` manages the registry, and the actual persistence access is in `codelet/napi/src/session_search_handler.rs`.

## Files To Create

- `codelet/tools/src/inject_summary.rs` — Tool struct, parameter/result types, handler type alias, global handler registry

## Files To Modify

- `codelet/tools/src/lib.rs` — Add module declaration, re-export tool and handler types, add `set_inject_summary_handler()` / `get_inject_summary_handler()` functions

## Acceptance Criteria

- Tool implements Rig Tool trait with correct name, description, schema
- JSON schema for parameters validates correctly
- Handler type alias and registry follow established pattern
- Tool returns error when no handler is registered (like SessionSearchTool does)
- Tool is registered in the tool list (lib.rs exports)

CMPCT-009.description:
Create `codelet/napi/src/inject_summary_handler.rs` — the NAPI handler that performs the actual session manipulation when the agent calls `inject_summary`. Register the handler in the agent loop setup alongside SessionSearch and Fspec handlers.

## Research Foundation

This implements the "partition → clear → restore → inject" pattern that makes the agent the sole authority over its own context compression. Focus (Verma, arXiv:2601.07190, Jan 2026) showed that agent autonomy over compression (22.7% token reduction, zero accuracy loss) outperforms external compression. HiAgent (Hu et al., ACL 2025) showed 2× success rate improvement when agents control their own memory boundaries.

The key insight from SimpleMem (Liu et al., ICLR 2026 Workshop LLA, arXiv:2601.02553) applies here: semantic density gating should be performed by the entity with the most context — which is the agent itself. inject_summary is how the agent's judgment materializes as persistent context.

## What To Build

A handler closure that captures `BackgroundSession`'s inner `Session` and, when invoked with DAG content:

1. **Partitions** `session.messages` using `partition_for_compaction()` from `codelet_cli::session::system_reminders` — cleanly separates system reminder messages (identified by `<system-reminder>` XML tags in `UserContent::Text`) from all other messages.

2. **Clears** `session.messages` entirely.

3. **Restores** only the system reminder messages (from step 1).

4. **Appends** the DAG content as a new `Message::User` wrapped in `<system-reminder>` with `<!-- type:compaction-dag -->` marker — making it part of the stable prefix for prompt caching and preserved through future compactions.

5. **Resets** `session.turns` to empty and updates `session.token_tracker` display values to reflect the new context size.

6. **Returns** `{ injected_tokens: u64, remaining_budget: u64 }` to the agent.

**Future integration note:** CMPCT-010 will add a `compaction_in_progress` flag to BackgroundSession. When that work is done, the inject_summary handler will be extended to clear that flag after injection completes, so subsequent SessionSearch calls return full (untrimmed) content.

## Existing Pattern to Follow

This is essentially the same mechanism as `execute_compaction()` in `codelet/cli/src/interactive_helpers.rs` (lines 170-303), which already does:
- `partition_for_compaction(&session.messages)` → extract system reminders
- `session.messages.clear()` → clear all messages
- `session.messages.extend(system_reminders)` → restore system reminders
- Append summary as `Message::User` → add compaction result

The difference: `inject_summary` replaces the LLM-generated summary with the agent-written DAG and skips kept-turns reconstruction (the DAG IS the kept context).

## Registration Point

In `codelet/napi/src/session_manager.rs`, the agent loop setup (around line 5365) already registers handlers:
```rust
// AMGR-001: Register SessionSearch handler for this session
let session_search_handler = crate::session_search_handler::create_handler(...);
codelet_tools::set_session_search_handler(session.id, Some(session_search_handler));
```

Add inject_summary handler registration immediately after, following the same pattern.

## Persistence Note

Builder turns (the SessionSearch calls and agent reasoning during DAG construction) ARE persisted to disk as they stream — `persist_user_message()` and `persist_assistant_message()` fire during normal agent execution. The builder turns are only dropped from the in-memory `session.messages`, not from the on-disk JSONL store. They remain recoverable via SessionSearch.

## Files To Create

- `codelet/napi/src/inject_summary_handler.rs` — Handler function `create_handler()` returning `InjectSummaryHandler` closure

## Files To Modify

- `codelet/napi/src/lib.rs` — Add module declaration
- `codelet/napi/src/session_manager.rs` — Register handler in agent loop setup (~line 5368), clean up handler on session teardown (~line 5576)

## Acceptance Criteria

- Handler correctly partitions, clears, restores system reminders, and injects DAG
- DAG content is wrapped in `<system-reminder><!-- type:compaction-dag -->` markers
- Builder turns are dropped from in-memory messages but NOT from persistence
- Token tracker is recalculated to reflect new context size
- Handler is registered and cleaned up alongside SessionSearch handler
- Returns accurate injected_tokens and remaining_budget values

CMPCT-010.description:
Extend `codelet/napi/src/session_search_handler.rs` to apply Layer 0 structurally lossless trimming to SessionSearch results during DAG construction. Add a `compaction_in_progress` flag to `BackgroundSession` that controls when trimming is active.

## Research Foundation

CMV (Santoni, Imperial College London, arXiv:2602.22402, Feb 2026) demonstrates that trimming applied to tool outputs before the agent processes them yields 20-86% token reduction. The critical insight is WHERE trimming happens: not on the stored data (originals are sacred), but on the RETRIEVAL PATH — the data the agent sees during DAG construction. This is "Option A" from the design document: implicit trimming via session state flag.

SimpleMem (Liu et al., ICLR 2026 Workshop LLA) validates this approach conceptually: their "Semantic Structured Compression" stage distills interactions into compact indexed units during the write phase. Our trimming serves the same purpose during the read/retrieval phase.

## What To Build

### 1. BackgroundSession Flag

Add `compaction_in_progress: Arc<AtomicBool>` field to `BackgroundSession` in `codelet/napi/src/session_manager.rs` (alongside existing fields like `compaction_progress: RwLock<Option<CompactionProgress>>`).

CMPCT-011.description:
Rewrite `execute_compaction()` in `codelet/cli/src/interactive_helpers.rs` to trigger the in-view DAG construction flow instead of the batch LLM approach. Create the compaction system instruction that guides the agent through DAG construction. Wire per-turn structural annotation detection into the stream loop.

## Research Foundation

This is the core integration card — where the three-layer architecture comes together. It implements the central thesis validated across all seven research papers:

- **LCM** (Ehrlich & Blackman, Voltropy PBC, Feb 2026): Hierarchical summary DAG with D0/D1/D2 depth levels. LCM-augmented agents outperform Claude Code on OOLONG long-context evaluation from 32K to 1M tokens.
- **Focus** (Verma, arXiv:2601.07190, Jan 2026): Agent-autonomous compression — the agent decides when and what to compress. 22.7% token reduction with identical accuracy.
- **HiAgent** (Hu et al., ACL 2025): Subgoal-based hierarchical working memory management — 2× success rate, 3.8 fewer steps.
- **ACON** (Kang et al., KAIST/Microsoft, arXiv:2510.00615, Oct 2025): Compression guidelines embedded in system instructions yield 26-54% peak token reduction while maintaining task performance.
- **H-MEM** (Sun & Zeng, arXiv:2507.22925, Jul 2025): Multi-level semantic abstraction with positional index routing — hierarchical organization is a NECESSARY CONDITION for robust long-term reasoning.

## What To Build

### 1. Rewrite execute_compaction()

Currently at `codelet/cli/src/interactive_helpers.rs` lines 170-310, `execute_compaction()` does:
1. `partition_for_compaction()` → separate system reminders
2. Create LLM prompt function via provider
3. Calculate summarization budget
4. Convert messages to turns
5. Call `compactor.compact()` → batch LLM anchor detection + LLM summary generation
6. Reconstruct messages: system reminders + kept turns + summary + continuation

New flow:
1. Set `compaction_in_progress` flag to `true` (triggers Layer 0 trimming in SessionSearch)
2. Execute `/clear` (clears in-memory context, reinjects system reminders, preserves persistence)
3. Inject compaction system instruction as the next user message — tells the agent to build its DAG via SessionSearch and call `inject_summary`
4. Return control to the agent loop — the agent takes over from here
5. Agent calls SessionSearch (gets trimmed results via Layer 0), builds DAG, calls inject_summary
6. `inject_summary` handler (CMPCT-009) performs the partition→clear→restore→inject and clears the flag

### 2. Compaction System Instruction

The system instruction that's injected after `/clear` to guide the agent. Must be concise (consumes context during rebuild):

```
Your context window was getting full. Your conversation history has been preserved on disk and is fully searchable via SessionSearch. Build a hierarchical summary DAG of your session:

1. Search strategically (not linearly):
   - SessionSearch(show, max_turns: 10) for recent context
   - SessionSearch(search, query: "error|failed|fix") for error resolutions
   - SessionSearch(search, query: "decision|chose|architecture") for decisions
   - SessionSearch(search, query: "TODO|blocker|question") for open items

2. Write a structured summary with depth levels:
   - D2 (Durable): Architecture decisions, milestones still in effect
   - D1 (Arc): What was attempted, outcomes, current work state
   - D0 (Detailed): Exact files, decisions, errors from recent work
   - Include [SessionSearch: turns X-Y] references for future drilldown

3. Call inject_summary(content) with your complete DAG to pin it and continue working.
```

### 3. Per-Turn Structural Annotation Detection

In `codelet/cli/src/interactive/stream_loop.rs`, after each completed turn:
- Inspect the turn's tool calls for fspec commands → `FspecMilestone`
- Detect error→success transitions → `ErrorResolution`
- Track Write/Edit tool calls → `FileModification`
- Attach annotations to the turn's metadata (zero cost, inline)

## Codebase Flow

```
stream_loop.rs (per-turn annotation detection)
  → compaction_hook detects threshold exceeded
  → execute_compaction() [rewritten]
    → set compaction_in_progress flag
    → clear_history() [existing, session_manager.rs:1574]
    → inject system instruction as user message
    → return to agent loop
  → agent calls SessionSearch (trimmed via CMPCT-010)
  → agent calls inject_summary (handled by CMPCT-009)
    → clears flag, pins DAG, drops builder turns
  → agent continues working normally
```

- Agent receives compaction system instruction and can build DAG via SessionSearch
- inject_summary is called and context is properly reconstructed
- Per-turn annotations are detected inline (zero cost)

CMPCT-012.description:
Modify the existing `CompactionHook` threshold trigger to use the in-view DAG construction flow instead of the batch LLM pipeline. This is the Layer 2 safety net — it fires when context hits 85-90% capacity and the agent hasn't proactively managed its context.

## Research Foundation

ACON (Kang et al., KAIST/Microsoft, arXiv:2510.00615, Oct 2025) demonstrates that compression guidelines optimized via failure analysis yield 26-54% peak token reduction while maintaining task performance. The emergency threshold acts as the failure-analysis trigger — when the agent doesn't compress proactively, the threshold forces it.

Focus (Verma, arXiv:2601.07190, Jan 2026) describes a "sawtooth" context pattern where context grows during exploration and collapses during consolidation. The emergency threshold prevents the sawtooth from hitting the ceiling by forcing a consolidation when the agent fails to initiate one.

## What To Build

### Current Flow (to be replaced)

In `codelet/core/src/compaction_hook.rs`, the `CompactionHook` detects when context usage exceeds the threshold. The post-stream-loop logic in `stream_loop.rs` checks `compaction_needed` and calls `execute_compaction()` which runs the batch LLM pipeline.

### New Flow

When the threshold is exceeded:
1. Auto-trigger `/clear` (same as manual, preserves persistence)
2. Set `compaction_in_progress` flag to `true`
3. Inject the compaction system instruction (same instruction as CMPCT-011)
4. The last user message is re-appended after the instruction so the agent knows what to resume
5. Agent builds DAG via SessionSearch, calls `inject_summary`, then continues

### Minimum Preserved Context

After emergency compaction, context contains at minimum:
- System reminders (CLAUDE.md, environment, fspec workflow)
- Injected DAG summary
- Last user message (so the agent knows what to do next)

Never drops below this floor.

### Proactive /compact Command

Also wire up a `/compact` slash command that the agent can call proactively when it notices context pressure. This triggers the same in-view flow but without the emergency urgency — the agent initiates it on its own terms.

## Codebase Integration Points

- `codelet/core/src/compaction_hook.rs` — Threshold detection logic (keep as-is, it's orthogonal)
- `codelet/cli/src/interactive/stream_loop.rs` — Post-turn compaction trigger (modify to use new flow)
- `codelet/napi/src/session_manager.rs` — `session_compact()` NAPI binding (modify to use new flow)

## Files To Modify

- `codelet/cli/src/interactive/stream_loop.rs` — Modify threshold-triggered compaction to use in-view flow
- `codelet/napi/src/session_manager.rs` — Modify `session_compact()` to use in-view flow

## Acceptance Criteria

- Last user message is preserved through emergency compaction
- Post-compaction context contains: system reminders + DAG + last user message
- /compact slash command triggers same flow proactively
- CompactionHook threshold detection logic is unchanged
- No separate LLM calls during emergency compaction
- Agent can resume working after emergency compaction without losing current task

CMPCT-013.description:
Remove the old batch LLM-based compaction infrastructure after the in-view DAG construction flow is validated and stable. This is the final migration phase — pure deletion, zero new functionality.

## Research Foundation

The old system embodies every antipattern identified by the research:

- **Flat summarization** contradicts H-MEM (Sun & Zeng, arXiv:2507.22925): hierarchical memory organization is a NECESSARY CONDITION for robust long-term reasoning. The old `generate_llm_summary()` produces flat prose.
- **External compression** contradicts Focus (Verma, arXiv:2601.07190) and HiAgent (Hu et al., ACL 2025): agents that control their own compression outperform agents compressed externally. The old system compresses the agent without its input.
- **Flaky heuristics** contradicts ACON (Kang et al., arXiv:2510.00615): `detect_build_status()` matching substrings "pass"/"fail" against arbitrary tool output produces silent misclassifications (false positives on "password", "bypass", `DB_PASS`). `extract_goal_from_message()` matching action verbs like "build", "remove", "please" in user messages.
- **Expensive batch calls** contradict CMV (Santoni, arXiv:2602.22402): the highest-ROI intervention is structural trimming (20-86% reduction at zero cost), not expensive LLM summarization.

- `extract_json_from_response()` — JSON extraction helper

- `LLM_TIMEOUT_SECS` constant — timeout configuration

Keep structural detection for annotations (per-turn, inline, zero-cost).

CMPCT-014.description: When compaction is active (isCompacting=true), pressing Esc does not stop the agent. The Esc handler in AgentView.tsx (Priority 5) only checks `displayIsLoading` (which comes from `rustSnapshot.isLoading`). During compaction, `isLoading` may be false while `isCompacting` is true, so the Esc key falls through to clear input or show exit confirmation instead of interrupting the session. The user sees '(Esc to stop)' in the compaction indicator but pressing Esc does nothing to stop compaction.

questions.answer: FspecTool should parse <system-reminder> tags from console/stderr output during TypeScript function execution and include them in the tool response. These provide timely workflow orchestration context that tells the LLM what needs to be done next, chaining the entire ACDD process together. The system reminders implement an anti-drift pattern that makes fspec more than just a CLI tool - it becomes an AI agent workflow orchestrator.
questions.text: @human: The fspec commands output system reminders to stderr via console.error() - how should these be captured and returned to the agent when called via NAPI? Should they be included in the tool response JSON?

questions.answer: The Tool::call() method should provide its own callback function that imports and executes the real fspec command modules from src/commands/. This avoids needing external callbacks. The Rust code creates the callback and passes it to callFspecCommand.

Should this callback be implemented as part of the Rust Tool::call() method, or should it be a separate TypeScript function that imports and executes the fspec commands?

questions.answer: No specific performance measurements required. The goal is simply to eliminate CLI process spawning overhead completely. As long as FspecTool calls TypeScript functions directly via NAPI without spawning processes, the performance improvement is sufficient. No complex caching strategies needed.
questions.text: @human: For performance optimization, should we pre-import all fspec command modules when FspecTool is initialized, or dynamically import them on each call? What about caching project state between calls?

CONFIG-005.description:
Currently TypeScript reads ~/.fspec/credentials/credentials.json and passes API keys to Rust at session creation time. This creates a stale credentials problem - if a user updates their API key via the TUI, existing Rust sessions don't pick up the new key.

Credential management should be handled entirely in Rust:
1. Rust reads ~/.fspec/credentials/credentials.json directly
2. Rust checks for updated credentials when making API calls (or on session resume)
3. TypeScript only saves/deletes credentials to the file - doesn't pass keys to NAPI
4. Eliminates stale credential problem
5. Single source of truth for credential resolution in Rust

CTX-002.description:
Implement OpenCode's compaction TRIGGER logic (when to compact, not how to compact).

**Issue 1: Token Counting (BROKEN)**
Current: `effective = input - (cache_read * 0.9)` - discounts cache, ignores output
OpenCode: `count = input + cache_read + output` - includes ALL tokens

**Issue 2: Threshold Calculation (SUBOPTIMAL)**  
Current: `threshold = context_window * 0.9` - static percentage
OpenCode: `usable = context_window - min(model_max_output, 32000)` - reserves output space

**Required Changes:**
1. Token count = input + cache_read + output (include all, no discount)
2. Threshold = context_window - min(model_max_output, SESSION_OUTPUT_MAX)
3. Add SESSION_OUTPUT_TOKEN_MAX = 32,000 constant
4. Add max_output_tokens to provider trait
5. Trigger when: count > usable

**Files to modify:**
- codelet/core/src/compaction_hook.rs (token calculation)
- codelet/cli/src/compaction_threshold.rs (threshold calculation)
- codelet/providers/src/lib.rs (add max_output_tokens trait method)

examples.text: Claude Sonnet (200k context, 8k max output): usable = 200,000 - min(8,192, 32,000) = 200,000 - 8,192 = 191,808 tokens
High-output model (200k context, 64k max output): usable = 200,000 - min(64,000, 32,000) = 200,000 - 32,000 = 168,000 tokens (SESSION_OUTPUT_MAX caps it)
Token counting: input=150,000 + cache_read=20,000 + output=5,000 = 175,000 total (NOT 150,000 - 18,000 = 132,000 as current code does)
Trigger check for Claude: total=175,000, usable=191,808 → 175,000 < 191,808 → NO compaction (current code would trigger at 180,000)
Trigger check for Claude: total=195,000, usable=191,808 → 195,000 > 191,808 → TRIGGER compaction
Unknown model (context=100k, max_output=0): min(0, 32000)=0, fallback to 32000 → usable = 100,000 - 32,000 = 68,000 tokens
Zero context window: context=0 → compaction returns false immediately (no context = no compaction)
Disable flag set: DISABLE_AUTOCOMPACT=true → compaction returns false immediately regardless of token count
Edge case: total exactly equals usable (191,808 == 191,808) → NO trigger (OpenCode uses > not >=)

rules.text: Token count MUST include input_tokens + cache_read_tokens + output_tokens (all three summed, no discounting)
Usable context MUST be calculated as: context_window - min(model_max_output, SESSION_OUTPUT_MAX)
SESSION_OUTPUT_TOKEN_MAX constant MUST be 32,000 tokens
Compaction MUST trigger when: (input + cache_read + output) > usable_context
Provider trait MUST expose max_output_tokens() method returning the model's maximum output token limit
When model_max_output is 0, MUST use SESSION_OUTPUT_TOKEN_MAX (32k) as fallback reservation
When context_window is 0, compaction MUST NOT trigger (return false immediately)
A configurable disable flag MUST allow skipping compaction entirely
Comparison MUST use strictly greater than (>), not greater-or-equal (>=)

examples.text: INITIAL RUN: Human runs 'fspec discover-foundation' → Command creates foundation.json.draft with structure → Draft has REQUIRED fields: project{name,vision,projectType}, problemSpace{primaryProblem{title,description,impact}}, solutionSpace{overview,capabilities[]}, personas[] → All fields contain [QUESTION: ...] or [DETECTED: ...] placeholders → Command emits system-reminder: 'Draft created. To complete foundation, you must ULTRATHINK the entire codebase. Analyze EVERYTHING: commands, routes, UI, tests, README, package.json. Understand HOW it works, then determine WHY it exists and WHAT users can do. I will guide you field-by-field. Field 1/9: project.name'

FIELD 1 (project.name): Command reads draft → Finds [QUESTION: What is the project name?] → Emits: 'Field 1/9: project.name. Analyze package.json name field. Confirm with human. Run: fspec update-foundation --field project.name --value <name>' → AI reads package.json, sees 'fspec' → AI asks human 'Package name is fspec, correct?' → Human confirms → AI runs 'fspec update-foundation --field project.name --value fspec' → Command detects update, re-scans draft, finds next unfilled field

FIELD 2 (project.vision): Command re-scans → Finds [QUESTION: What is the one-sentence vision?] → Emits: 'Field 2/9: project.vision (elevator pitch). ULTRATHINK: Read ALL code, understand the system deeply. What is the core PURPOSE? Focus on WHY this exists, not HOW it works. Ask human. Run: fspec update-foundation --field project.vision --value "your vision"' → AI reads README, analyzes commands (validate, format, list-features), understands it manages Gherkin specs → AI formulates: 'CLI tool for managing Gherkin specifications using ACDD' → AI asks human 'Is vision correct?' → Human confirms → AI updates field

FIELD 3 (project.projectType): Command re-scans → Finds [DETECTED: cli-tool] → Emits: 'Field 3/9: project.projectType. Auto-detected cli-tool from commander.js usage and bin field. Verify with human. Options: cli-tool, web-app, library, sdk, mobile-app, desktop-app, service, api, other. Run: fspec update-foundation --field project.projectType --value cli-tool' → AI analyzes code: sees commander.js imports, .command() calls, bin field in package.json → AI confirms: yes, this is cli-tool → AI asks human 'Detected cli-tool, correct?' → Human confirms → AI updates field → Command chains to problemSpace

FIELD 4 (problemSpace.primaryProblem): Command re-scans → Finds [QUESTION: What problem does this solve?] → Emits: 'Field 4/9: problemSpace.primaryProblem. CRITICAL: Think from USER perspective. WHO uses this (persona)? WHAT problem do THEY face? WHY do they need this solution? Analyze codebase to understand user pain, ask human. Required: title, description, impact (high/medium/low). Run: fspec update-foundation --field problemSpace.primaryProblem.title --value "Problem Title"' → AI analyzes: this is CLI for specs, users are developers, they need structured spec workflow → AI asks human 'Primary problem: Developers lack structured workflow for managing specifications?' → Human elaborates → AI updates title,description,impact

FIELD 5 (solutionSpace.capabilities): Command re-scans → Finds [QUESTION: What can users DO?] → Emits: 'Field 5/9: solutionSpace.capabilities. List 3-7 HIGH-LEVEL abilities users have. Focus on WHAT not HOW. Example: "Spec Validation" (WHAT), not "Uses Cucumber parser" (HOW). Analyze commands/features to identify user-facing capabilities. Run: fspec update-foundation --field solutionSpace.capabilities[0].name --value "Capability Name"' → AI analyzes commands: validate, format, list, create → Groups into capabilities: Spec Management, Validation, Work Unit Tracking → AI asks human → Human confirms → AI adds each capability with description

FIELD 6 (personas): Command re-scans → Finds [QUESTION: Who uses this?] → Emits: 'Field 6/9: personas. Identify ALL user types from interactions. CLI tools: who runs commands? Web apps: who uses UI + who calls API? Analyze ALL user-facing code. Ask human about goals and pain points. Run: fspec update-foundation --field personas[0].name --value "Persona Name"' → AI analyzes: CLI commands used by developers, no web UI, no API consumers → Identifies persona: "Developer using CLI in terminal" → AI asks human about goals: managing specs, following ACDD → AI asks about pain points: fragmented tools, no workflow → AI updates persona with name, description, goals, painPoints

COMPLETION: AI fills last required field → Command re-scans → ALL required fields complete (no [QUESTION:] in required fields) → Command validates draft against JSON schema → Schema validation PASSES → Command creates spec/foundation.json from draft → Command deletes spec/foundation.json.draft → Command AUTOMATICALLY runs 'fspec generate-foundation-md' (no AI action needed) → Command emits: 'Discovery complete\! Created: spec/foundation.json, spec/FOUNDATION.md. Foundation is ready. You can now run fspec commands that require foundation.' → AI can now proceed with other work

ERROR: Manual Editing → AI uses Write tool to edit foundation.json.draft directly → Command detects: draft mtime changed without fspec command → Command compares last known state vs current → Command emits ERROR in system-reminder: 'CRITICAL: You manually edited foundation.json.draft. This violates the workflow. You MUST use: fspec update-foundation --field <path> --value <value>. Reverting your changes. Draft restored to last valid state. Try again with proper command.' → Draft is restored → AI must use fspec commands

ERROR: Validation Failure → AI fills all fields → Command validates against schema → Validation FAILS: missing required field problemSpace.primaryProblem.description → Command emits: 'Schema validation failed. Missing required: problemSpace.primaryProblem.description. Draft NOT finalized. Fix by running: fspec update-foundation --field problemSpace.primaryProblem.description --value "your description". Then re-run discover-foundation to validate.' → Draft kept, foundation.json NOT created → AI fixes missing field and re-runs

examples.text: In bootstrap docs, Step 3 is 'Big Picture Event Storming (Foundation Level)' and Step 4 is 'Event Storm - Domain Discovery BEFORE Example Mapping'. After renaming to 'Foundation Event Storm' and 'Feature Event Storm' with comparison table, the distinction is immediately clear from names alone.

AI is about to do Feature Event Storm but hasn't seen the codebase yet. Instead of guessing, AI first runs 'fspec research --tool=ast --files src/auth/*.ts' to understand authentication domain. Then shares findings: 'I found 3 domain events: UserRegistered, LoginAttempted, SessionExpired. Should we do Feature Event Storm to map the full authentication flow?' AI reads 'coverage files are automatically synchronized' and thinks linking is also automatic. Wastes time waiting for coverage to auto-populate. With ✨ AUTOMATIC vs 🔧 MANUAL labels, AI immediately sees: ✨ AUTOMATIC: create-feature creates .coverage files, delete-scenario syncs coverage. 🔧 MANUAL: link-coverage --test-file required to link tests. AI runs the right commands without confusion.

With clarification that parser extracts ONLY step.text, AI correctly writes: // @step Given I have the following items: (table content ignored by matcher).

AI fills field 3 of foundation discovery, then realizes field 1 (project name) was wrong. Without iteration docs, AI might think 'too late, can't go back'. With explicit iteration documentation, AI confidently runs 'fspec update-foundation projectName "correct-name"' to fix the mistake, then continues from field 4.

architectureNotes.text: Service worker runs a Streamable HTTP MCP server using offscreen document or chrome.sockets API for TCP listening. Alternatives: use chrome.offscreen to create a hidden page that runs the HTTP server, or use a tiny Node.js bridge process spawned alongside

Content script injects into all pages and monitors navigator.modelContext for tool registrations. Uses MutationObserver-like pattern or polls for changes. Communicates with service worker via chrome.runtime.sendMessage

Architecture layers: Content Script (WebMCP tool discovery per tab) → Service Worker (tool registry, browser control APIs, event aggregation) → MCP HTTP Server (Streamable HTTP transport with SSE for notifications) → ConnectMCP (fspec agent client)

MV3 service workers cannot open TCP ports directly. The HTTP server MUST run in either: (a) an offscreen document (chrome.offscreen API), (b) a companion Node.js native messaging host process, or (c) use the chrome.sockets API (if available in MV3). Option (b) is most reliable and follows the mcp-chrome pattern

For bidirectional events via ConnectMCP: ConnectMCP's rmcp ClientHandler has on_tool_list_changed callback. When the extension sends MCP notifications/tools/list_changed, rmcp re-fetches tools. For custom browser events, use MCP notifications with custom method names that get injected into the session via watcher_input_tx

Content scripts run in an ISOLATED WORLD — they share the page's DOM but NOT the page's JavaScript context. navigator.modelContext is only accessible from the page's MAIN world. To bridge this, use chrome.scripting.executeScript({ world: 'MAIN' }) to inject scripts into the page context. These main-world scripts communicate back via window.postMessage(), which the content script relays to the service worker via chrome.runtime.sendMessage.

Architecture layers: Main-World Injected Script (WebMCP tool discovery/invocation per tab, runs in page context) → Content Script (isolated world relay, postMessage ↔ chrome.runtime bridge) → Service Worker (tool registry, browser control APIs, event aggregation, native messaging client) → Native Messaging Host (Node.js, runs Streamable HTTP MCP server with GET-based SSE for persistent notifications) → ConnectMCP (fspec agent client)

EXT-001.description: Build a Chrome extension (Manifest V3) that leverages WebMCP (navigator.modelContext API) and exposes browser capabilities as an MCP server. The extension lives in the extension/ directory and is connectable via ConnectMCP tool using Streamable HTTP transport. It must be bidirectional: the agent can invoke browser tools AND the browser extension can fire events/notifications back to the agent session via MCP server-initiated messages (SSE channel). The extension bridges the gap between WebMCP's in-browser tool registration and fspec's ConnectMCP-based MCP client, enabling the agent to discover and call WebMCP tools registered by any website, control tabs/navigation, capture screenshots, and receive page-level events (navigation, tool registration changes, DOM mutations) as real-time notifications.

architectureNotes.text: Native host is pure Node.js with zero npm dependencies — uses only built-in http, net, crypto, path, os, fs modules. This keeps it lightweight and avoids npm install for the host process.

Chrome native messaging protocol: messages are length-prefixed (4-byte unsigned 32-bit little-endian integer) followed by raw JSON bytes. The host reads stdin in this format and writes stdout in this format. Max message size is 1MB.

The MCP Streamable HTTP server uses Node.js built-in http module. SSE streams are implemented by keeping the response open with Transfer-Encoding: chunked and writing 'data: {...}\n\n' formatted lines. Each SSE event is a JSON-RPC notification or response.

Tool call routing: when a POST /mcp tools/call arrives, the host writes a native messaging frame to stdout addressed to the extension. The host assigns a correlation ID and holds the HTTP response open until the extension replies on stdin with a matching correlation ID. This is an async request-response pattern over the native messaging channel.

assumptions: The Chrome extension ID is known at registration time — the user provides it via --extension-id flag during --register
The native host process is long-lived — Chrome keeps it alive as long as the extension has an active connectNative() port. It does not need to auto-start on system boot.
EXT-003.description: Build the Node.js native messaging host process that: (a) registers with Chrome as a native messaging host, (b) runs a Streamable HTTP MCP server on port 19876, (c) implements the full MCP lifecycle (POST initialize, GET SSE stream, POST tools/call, DELETE session), (d) communicates with the Chrome extension service worker via stdin/stdout native messaging protocol.

examples.text: Agent calls ConnectMCP(transport: 'http', url: 'http://localhost:19876/mcp') → POST /mcp with initialize → server returns {serverInfo, capabilities, protocolVersion} with Mcp-Session-Id header → tools/list returns empty list (no extension connected yet)

Extension calls chrome.runtime.connectNative('com.fspec.webmcp') → host starts, reads 4-byte length prefix + JSON from stdin → host parses as native messaging frame → when extension sends {type: 'TOOLS_CHANGED', tools: [...]}, host updates internal tool registry

Agent opens GET /mcp with Accept: text/event-stream → server responds 200 with Content-Type: text/event-stream → stream stays open → when extension sends browser event via stdin, host writes SSE data line with JSON-RPC notification → agent receives it

Agent sends POST /mcp with tools/call for browser_navigate → host writes native messaging frame to stdout for the extension → extension executes chrome.tabs.update → extension writes result back on stdin → host returns JSON-RPC result to agent
Agent sends DELETE /mcp with Mcp-Session-Id → server closes SSE stream for that session → cleans up session state → returns 200

User runs node extension/host/native-host.js --register → script detects macOS → writes com.fspec.webmcp.json to ~/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/NativeMessagingHosts/ with correct path and allowed_origins
POST /mcp without Mcp-Session-Id for a non-initialize request → server responds 400 Bad Request with error message
POST /mcp with invalid Mcp-Session-Id → server responds 404 Not Found (session does not exist)

rules.text: The native messaging host MUST be a standalone Node.js script that Chrome launches via chrome.runtime.connectNative('com.fspec.webmcp')
The host process communicates with the Chrome extension via stdin/stdout using Chrome's native messaging protocol (4-byte little-endian length prefix + JSON payload)
The host MUST run a Streamable HTTP MCP server on port 19876 (default) at endpoint /mcp
MCP lifecycle: POST /mcp for JSON-RPC requests (initialize, tools/list, tools/call), GET /mcp for persistent SSE notification stream, DELETE /mcp for session termination
The server MUST assign an Mcp-Session-Id header on initialize response and require it on all subsequent requests

The host MUST support a --register flag that writes the Chrome native messaging host manifest JSON to the platform-specific directory (macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/NativeMessagingHosts/)
The host MUST relay messages bidirectionally: MCP requests from HTTP clients are forwarded to the extension via stdout, and extension responses from stdin are returned to the HTTP client
The GET /mcp SSE stream MUST stay open for the duration of the session to enable server-initiated notifications (browser events pushed from extension → native host → SSE → agent)
The native host lives in extension/host/ directory with its own entry point script, separate from the extension's browser-side code
The host MUST handle multiple concurrent MCP sessions (multiple agents connecting simultaneously) by tracking session IDs

EXT-003.title: Native Messaging Host & MCP Streamable HTTP Server

userStory.action: connect to the Chrome extension's MCP server via ConnectMCP and have tool calls and notifications routed through a native messaging host
userStory.benefit: the agent can invoke browser tools and receive real-time browser events through the standard MCP protocol without Chrome service worker TCP limitations

architectureNotes.text: chrome.runtime.connectNative() in MV3 service workers returns a Port object. Messages are sent/received as plain JSON objects (Chrome handles the native messaging frame encoding/decoding). The service worker does NOT need to do 4-byte length-prefix framing — that's the native host's responsibility. The Port.postMessage() and Port.onMessage handle serialization.

Message type taxonomy: FSPEC_WEBMCP_TOOL_REGISTERED, FSPEC_WEBMCP_TOOL_UNREGISTERED (content→SW for tool registry updates), FSPEC_INVOKE_TOOL, FSPEC_INVOKE_RESULT (SW→content→main and back for tool invocations), FSPEC_GET_STATUS (popup→SW for status queries), TOOL_CALL (native host→SW for incoming tool calls), TOOLS_CHANGED/NOTIFICATION (SW→native host for outgoing state changes)

The sender object in chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener automatically includes sender.tab.id for content scripts. No need for content scripts to manually include tab ID — Chrome provides it. Service worker uses sender.tab.id to route responses back.

EXT-004.description: Implement the Chrome extension service worker as the central event hub: tool registry management, chrome.runtime messaging between content scripts and service worker, window.postMessage relay in content scripts (isolated world ↔ main world bridge), and native messaging client connection to the host process. Content scripts act as relay between main-world injected scripts and the service worker.

examples.text: Extension loads → service worker calls chrome.runtime.connectNative('com.fspec.webmcp') → native host stdin/stdout connection established → service worker logs 'Native messaging connected'

Native host sends {type: 'TOOL_CALL', correlationId: 'abc', method: 'tools/call', params: {name: 'browser_navigate', arguments: {url: 'https://example.com'}}} via stdin → service worker receives and routes to chrome.tabs.update handler → handler returns result → service worker writes {correlationId: 'abc', result: {url: 'https://example.com', title: 'Example'}} to native port

Content script on tab 42 receives window.postMessage({type: 'FSPEC_WEBMCP_TOOL_REGISTERED', tool: {name: 'searchFlights', ...}}) from main-world script → content script calls chrome.runtime.sendMessage({type: 'FSPEC_WEBMCP_TOOL_REGISTERED', tool: {...}}) → service worker receives with sender.tab.id = 42 → updates tool registry → forwards TOOLS_CHANGED to native host

Service worker needs to invoke WebMCP tool on tab 42 → sends chrome.tabs.sendMessage(42, {type: 'FSPEC_INVOKE_TOOL', correlationId: 'xyz', toolName: 'searchFlights', args: {...}}) → content script receives → posts to main world via window.postMessage → main world executes tool → result flows back: postMessage → content script → chrome.runtime.sendMessage → service worker
Native messaging port disconnects (host process dies) → service worker detects port.onDisconnect → waits 2 seconds → retries chrome.runtime.connectNative → reconnects successfully
Popup sends chrome.runtime.sendMessage({type: 'FSPEC_GET_STATUS'}) → service worker responds with {connected: true, port: 19876, toolCount: 5, nativeConnected: true}

rules.text: Service worker MUST connect to native host via chrome.runtime.connectNative('com.fspec.webmcp') on startup and maintain the connection
Service worker MUST maintain a tool registry (Map of tool name → tool metadata) updated by native host TOOLS_CHANGED messages and content script WebMCP discovery messages

Content script MUST relay messages bidirectionally: window.postMessage (main world) ↔ chrome.runtime.sendMessage (service worker) using FSPEC_WEBMCP_ prefix for main→SW and FSPEC_INVOKE_ prefix for SW→main
Service worker MUST route incoming native host tool calls to the correct tab's content script and return the result back to the native host via native messaging
All messages between service worker and native host use the 4-byte little-endian length-prefix protocol (same as EXT-003 native messaging format)
Service worker MUST handle native messaging port disconnect gracefully and attempt reconnection
Messages from content scripts MUST include the sender tab ID so the service worker can route responses back to the correct tab

Service worker MUST forward browser event notifications (from chrome.tabs.onUpdated, onCreated, onRemoved) to the native host for SSE broadcast — actual event handlers are EXT-007 scope but the forwarding mechanism is EXT-004

EXT-004.title: Service Worker & Content Script Message Routing

userStory.action: have the service worker and content scripts route messages between the native host, browser APIs, and main-world scripts
userStory.benefit: downstream features (browser control, WebMCP discovery, events, popup) can use a reliable messaging backbone without each implementing their own routing

architectureNotes.text: Tool handlers are implemented as a new module (background/browser-tools.ts) that exports a function registry (Map<string, handler>). The message router's handleNativeMessage method is updated to check the native tool registry before returning 'no handler' errors.
For tools that need to resolve 'active tab' when no tabId is given, use chrome.tabs.query({active: true, currentWindow: true}) to find the current tab. This is a promise-based API in MV3.

The NATIVE_TOOLS definition in the native host (host/lib/mcp-server.mjs) must be expanded with the 7 new tools (browser_switch_tab, browser_close_tab, browser_get_page_content, browser_click_element, browser_fill_form, browser_go_back, browser_go_forward) so tools/list returns all 11.

chrome.scripting.executeScript returns a Promise<InjectionResult[]>. The results[0].result contains the actual return value. Need to handle serialization properly — complex DOM objects cannot be returned, only JSON-serializable values.

assumptions: All Chrome extension APIs are async in MV3. Tool handlers must be async functions. The TOOL_CALL handling in the message router must become asynchronous to support awaiting Chrome API results before sending the response back to the native host.
EXT-005.description: Implement the suite of browser control MCP tools: browser_navigate, browser_screenshot, browser_get_page_content, browser_list_tabs, browser_switch_tab, browser_close_tab, browser_click_element, browser_fill_form, browser_execute_script, browser_go_back, browser_go_forward. Each tool is exposed via the MCP server and executed via Chrome extension APIs (chrome.tabs, chrome.scripting, etc).

examples.text: Agent calls browser_navigate({url: 'https://example.com'}) → service worker calls chrome.tabs.update(activeTabId, {url: 'https://example.com'}) → waits for onUpdated with status 'complete' → returns {url: 'https://example.com', title: 'Example Domain'}

Agent calls browser_screenshot({tabId: 42}) → service worker calls chrome.tabs.captureVisibleTab(windowId, {format: 'png'}) → returns {content: [{type: 'image', data: 'iVBOR...', mimeType: 'image/png'}]}

Agent calls browser_list_tabs() → service worker calls chrome.tabs.query({}) → returns [{id: 1, url: 'https://example.com', title: 'Example', active: true}, {id: 2, url: 'about:blank', title: 'New Tab', active: false}]
Agent calls browser_execute_script({code: 'document.title'}) → service worker calls chrome.scripting.executeScript({target: {tabId}, func: ...}) → returns the script result as text

Agent calls browser_click_element({selector: '#submit-btn'}) → service worker injects script via chrome.scripting.executeScript → script finds element, calls click() → returns {clicked: true, selector: '#submit-btn'}
Agent calls browser_click_element({selector: '#nonexistent'}) → script cannot find element → returns MCP error {isError: true, content: [{type: 'text', text: 'Element not found: #nonexistent'}]}

Agent calls browser_fill_form({selector: '#email', value: 'test@example.com'}) → script sets input value and dispatches input+change events → returns {filled: true, selector: '#email', value: 'test@example.com'}
Agent calls browser_switch_tab({tabId: 42}) → service worker calls chrome.tabs.update(42, {active: true}) and chrome.windows.update(windowId, {focused: true}) → returns confirmation with tab info
Agent calls browser_close_tab({tabId: 42}) → service worker gets tab info first, then calls chrome.tabs.remove(42) → returns {closed: true, tabId: 42, url: 'https://example.com'}
Agent calls browser_get_page_content({tabId: 42, format: 'text'}) → returns page innerText; browser_get_page_content({format: 'html'}) → returns outerHTML
Agent calls browser_go_back() → chrome.tabs.goBack(activeTabId) → returns {navigated: true, direction: 'back'}; browser_go_forward() similarly

rules.text: Each browser control tool is registered as a native tool handler in the service worker, dispatched by the message router when a TOOL_CALL arrives from the native host with a matching tool name
browser_navigate uses chrome.tabs.update({url}) on the specified tab (or active tab if none specified) and returns the final URL and page title after load completes
browser_screenshot uses chrome.tabs.captureVisibleTab() and returns the screenshot as a base64-encoded PNG data URI
browser_list_tabs uses chrome.tabs.query({}) and returns an array of tab objects with id, url, title, and active status
browser_switch_tab uses chrome.tabs.update(tabId, {active: true}) and chrome.windows.update(windowId, {focused: true}) to focus the specified tab
browser_close_tab uses chrome.tabs.remove(tabId) and returns confirmation with the closed tab's info
browser_get_page_content uses chrome.scripting.executeScript to retrieve document.title, document.URL, and DOM content (innerText or outerHTML) from the specified tab
browser_click_element uses chrome.scripting.executeScript to find an element by CSS selector and call element.click() in the page context
browser_fill_form uses chrome.scripting.executeScript to find an element by CSS selector, set its value, and dispatch input/change events
browser_execute_script uses chrome.scripting.executeScript to run arbitrary JavaScript code in the specified tab and returns the result
browser_go_back and browser_go_forward use chrome.tabs.goBack(tabId) and chrome.tabs.goForward(tabId) respectively to navigate browser history
All tool results follow MCP content format: {content: [{type: 'text', text: '...'}]} for text results or {content: [{type: 'image', data: '...', mimeType: 'image/png'}]} for screenshots
Tools that accept an optional tabId default to the current active tab if no tabId is provided
The NATIVE_TOOLS array in the MCP server must be expanded to include all 11 tools with complete inputSchema definitions so tools/list returns them all
Tool handler errors (element not found, invalid selector, tab not found) must return MCP error responses with descriptive messages, not throw uncaught exceptions

EXT-005.title: Native Browser Control Tools

userStory.action: invoke browser control tools via the MCP connection
userStory.benefit: I can navigate pages, capture screenshots, list and manage tabs, execute scripts, interact with page elements, and control browser history programmatically

architectureNotes.text: The main-world discovery script runs as a self-contained function injected via chrome.scripting.executeScript({world: 'MAIN'}). It must monkey-patch navigator.modelContext to intercept registerTool/unregisterTool calls before any page scripts run. The script maintains a Map of registered tools keyed by name, and communicates exclusively via window.postMessage with FSPEC_ prefixed message types.

The message-router.ts tool name format must change from 'webmcp__<name>' to 'webmcp__<origin>__<name>' to match the MCP namespacing convention. The origin is the hostname extracted from the page URL. The content script relay already passes origin from the main-world postMessage.

Injection is triggered by chrome.tabs.onUpdated with status 'complete' in the service worker. A new webmcp-injector.ts module handles injection via chrome.scripting.executeScript({target: {tabId}, world: 'MAIN', func: discoveryFunction}). The discovery function is the serialized form of the main-world script.

EXT-006.description: Implement WebMCP tool discovery and invocation through main-world script injection. Discovery: inject scripts via chrome.scripting.executeScript({world: 'MAIN'}) to detect navigator.modelContext.registerTool/unregisterTool calls, relay tool metadata back via postMessage → content script → service worker. Invocation: inject main-world scripts to call tool execute() functions in page context, relay results back through the same chain. Tools namespaced as webmcp__<origin>__<toolName>. Requires Chrome 146+ with WebMCP flag.

examples.text: Site at travel-demo.bandarra.me registers tool 'searchFlights' → discovery script posts {type: FSPEC_WEBMCP_TOOL_REGISTERED, tool: {name: 'searchFlights', ...}, origin: 'travel-demo.bandarra.me'} → content script relays to SW → SW registers as 'webmcp__travel-demo.bandarra.me__searchFlights' → native host gets TOOLS_CHANGED → SSE notification to agent

Site at example.com unregisters tool 'oldTool' → discovery script posts {type: FSPEC_WEBMCP_TOOL_UNREGISTERED, toolName: 'oldTool', origin: 'example.com'} → content script relays → SW removes 'webmcp__example.com__oldTool' from registry → TOOLS_CHANGED → SSE notification

Agent calls tools/call with name 'webmcp__example.com__submitForm' and args {name: 'John'} → SW looks up tool in registry (source: webmcp, tabId: 42) → sends FSPEC_INVOKE_TOOL to tab 42's content script → content script posts to main world → main world calls the tool's execute({name: 'John'}) → result posted back → content script relays FSPEC_INVOKE_RESULT to SW → SW returns to native host
Tool execute() throws Error('Network timeout') → discovery script catches, posts {type: FSPEC_INVOKE_RESULT, correlationId: 'xyz', error: 'Network timeout'} → SW returns error response to agent

rules.text: Main-world discovery script MUST intercept navigator.modelContext.registerTool() and unregisterTool() calls by monkey-patching the API before any page script runs
WebMCP tools MUST be namespaced as webmcp__<origin>__<toolName> where origin is the hostname of the registering page
Discovery script injection MUST use chrome.scripting.executeScript with world: 'MAIN' to run in the page's JavaScript context
Tool invocation MUST relay through postMessage (main world) → content script → chrome.runtime → service worker → native host, and results flow back through the same chain in reverse
Tool registration MUST include the tool's name, description, inputSchema, origin (hostname), and tabId
When a website unregisters a tool, the extension MUST remove it from the registry and send notifications/tools/list_changed via SSE
Discovery script MUST be injected into every page on document_idle or tab complete, not just WebMCP-enabled sites (since we cannot know in advance which sites use WebMCP)
Tool invocation errors from execute() MUST be caught and returned as MCP error responses, not silently swallowed

EXT-006.title: WebMCP Tool Discovery & Invocation

userStory.action: discover and invoke WebMCP tools registered by websites
userStory.benefit: I can use web-page-provided tools like searchFlights or submitForm through the standard MCP protocol

architectureNotes.text: New module: browser-events.ts in src/background/ — captures Chrome event listeners and formats MCP notifications
Uses dependency injection for chrome.tabs so event listeners are testable without Chrome runtime
The MCP server already handles NOTIFICATION messages (mcp-server.mjs:180-189) — no changes needed on server side
messageRouter.forwardNotification() wraps event in {type:'NOTIFICATION', notification:{...}} envelope — already implemented

EXT-007.description: Implement server-initiated MCP notifications pushed to the agent via the GET-based SSE stream. Events: notifications/browser/navigation (chrome.tabs.onUpdated), notifications/browser/tab_created, notifications/browser/tab_closed, notifications/tools/list_changed (WebMCP registry changes), notifications/browser/load_complete. Service worker captures Chrome events, forwards to native host, host writes JSON-RPC notifications to SSE stream.

examples.text: User navigates tab 123 to https://new-page.com → agent receives SSE data: {jsonrpc:'2.0', method:'notifications/browser/navigation', params:{tabId:123, url:'https://new-page.com', title:'New Page'}}
User opens a new tab → agent receives SSE data: {jsonrpc:'2.0', method:'notifications/browser/tab_created', params:{tabId:456, url:'chrome://newtab', title:'New Tab'}}
User closes tab 123 → agent receives SSE data: {jsonrpc:'2.0', method:'notifications/browser/tab_closed', params:{tabId:123}}
Tab 123 finishes loading a page → agent receives SSE data: {jsonrpc:'2.0', method:'notifications/browser/load_complete', params:{tabId:123, url:'https://example.com', title:'Example'}}
WebMCP tool registered on a website → agent receives SSE data: {jsonrpc:'2.0', method:'notifications/tools/list_changed'} (already works via TOOLS_CHANGED)
Tab closed that had WebMCP tools → tools are unregistered AND both tab_closed and tools/list_changed notifications fire

rules.text: Service worker listens to chrome.tabs.onUpdated and forwards navigation events with tabId, url, title
Service worker listens to chrome.tabs.onCreated and forwards tab_created events with tabId, url, title
Service worker listens to chrome.tabs.onRemoved and forwards tab_closed events with tabId
Service worker fires notifications/browser/load_complete when tab status changes to 'complete'
notifications/tools/list_changed is already implemented via TOOLS_CHANGED message type in the MCP server
All notifications use JSON-RPC 2.0 format: { jsonrpc: '2.0', method: 'notifications/browser/...', params: {...} }
Notifications flow: Chrome event → service worker listener → messageRouter.forwardNotification() → native host stdin → MCP server → SSE stream → agent
The MCP server handleNativeMessage already broadcasts NOTIFICATION type messages to all SSE streams

EXT-007.title: Bidirectional Browser Event Notifications

userStory.action: receive real-time browser event notifications via the MCP SSE stream
userStory.benefit: I can react to navigation changes, tab lifecycle events, and tool availability without polling

architectureNotes.text: Extend StatusResponse in types/index.ts to include clientCount and tools array. Popup.ts uses chrome.runtime.sendMessage to query. Message router returns enriched data from toolRegistry.getAll() grouped by source.

Client count is tracked by native host MCP server (active SSE streams). Service worker requests it via native messaging and caches. For MVP, service worker can report 0 if count not yet pushed by native host.

EXT-008.description: Build the Chrome extension popup UI showing: server status (listening/stopped), configured port number, count of connected MCP clients, list of available tools grouped by source (native browser tools vs WebMCP tools per tab). Popup communicates with service worker via chrome.runtime.sendMessage to get current state.

examples.text: Native host connected, 2 MCP clients, 5 native tools + 3 WebMCP tools across 2 tabs → popup shows 'listening', port 19876, 2 clients, tools grouped as 'Browser Tools (5)' and 'example.com (2)' and 'app.test.io (1)'
Native host disconnected, no clients, no tools → popup shows 'stopped' with red dot, port 19876, 0 clients, empty tools section
Native host connected but no WebMCP tools → popup shows only 'Browser Tools' section with native tools listed

rules.text: Popup communicates with service worker via chrome.runtime.sendMessage using FSPEC_GET_STATUS message type
Server status displays as 'listening' when native host is connected, 'stopped' when disconnected
Tools are grouped by source: native browser tools in one section, WebMCP tools grouped by tab origin
Status response from service worker must include tools array with source and origin metadata for grouping
Status indicator dot is green for listening, red for stopped
Client count comes from the native host connection tracking the number of active MCP SSE streams

userStory.action: open the extension popup and see server status, port, clients, and available tools grouped by source
userStory.benefit: I can quickly verify the extension is connected and see what tools are available

architectureNotes.text: Layered discovery in webmcp-discovery.ts: Layer 1 navigator.modelContext (existing), Layer 2 WebMCP.prototype interception, Layer 3 post-load snapshot, Layer 4 ModelContextTesting (opportunistic). manifest.json run_at changed to document_start. Injector uses injectImmediately: true.

EXT-009.description:
When a website uses the WebMCP polyfill library (e.g., webmcp.dev's `new WebMCP().registerTool(...)`) instead of the native `navigator.modelContext.registerTool()` API, the fspec extension's monkey-patch interceptor never fires. Dynamically registered tools are invisible to the MCP client.

Three failure modes identified:
1. Polyfill bypass: webmcp.dev uses `WebMCP` class with its own internal registry — never touches `navigator.modelContext`
2. Injection race: MAIN-world script injected at `document_idle`/`complete` can miss tools registered during initial page script execution
3. Format mismatch: Tool entries from `TOOLS_CHANGED` may not match MCP `tools/list` expected shape

See `mcp-research.md` for full analysis, Chromium source references, and resolution plan.

examples.text: Site uses new WebMCP().registerTool('calculator', ...) — tool appears in MCP tools/list
Site uses navigator.modelContext.registerTool({name: 'weather'}) — tool appears in MCP tools/list (existing behavior)
Site registers tool during initial script execution before document_idle — tool still discovered via early injection
Site assigns window.webMCP = new WebMCP() after page load — Object.defineProperty trap catches it and wraps registerTool
WebMCP tools registered before extension injection are discovered via post-load snapshot of window.webMCP.getTools()
Tool registered via WebMCP library can be invoked through MCP and the execute callback fires in page context
Discovery script injected twice on same page only runs once (double-injection guard)
When ModelContextTesting is available, ontoolchange fires and listTools() catches tools registered before injection

rules.text: The discovery script must intercept navigator.modelContext.registerTool() for native Chrome WebMCP API and W3C-compliant polyfills
The discovery script must intercept WebMCP class prototype registerTool() for polyfill libraries that bypass navigator.modelContext
A post-load snapshot must scan well-known globals (window.webMCP, window.mcp) to discover tools registered before injection
Content script must run at document_start (not document_idle) to avoid missing early tool registrations
The MAIN-world script must be injected as early as possible using injectImmediately when available
Double-injection guard must prevent the same discovery script from running twice on the same page
Tool execute callbacks must be captured from all discovery layers so invocation works regardless of registration source
If ModelContextTesting API is available (WebMCPTesting flag enabled), prefer its ontoolchange event and listTools() over monkey-patching

EXT-009.title: WebMCP dynamic tool registration not detected — polyfill libraries bypass navigator.modelContext

userStory.action: have WebMCP tools discovered regardless of how the page registers them
userStory.benefit: I can use dynamically registered tools from any WebMCP-compatible website

architectureNotes.text: Replace eval()-based execution in browser-tools.ts with chrome.userScripts.execute() using USER_SCRIPT world. Add ChromeUserScriptsForTools interface to deps. Call configureWorld() in service-worker.ts on startup. Add userScripts permission to manifest.json.

EXT-010.description:
browser_execute_script always returns "null" regardless of the code passed. The handler uses chrome.scripting.executeScript with a func that calls eval(codeStr), but MV3's Content Security Policy forbids unsafe-eval in the extension's isolated world. The eval() silently throws an EvalError which Chromium catches and returns null. Other browser tools (get_page_content, click_element, fill_form) work fine because they use inline function code without eval.

Fix: Replace eval()-based execution with chrome.userScripts API (Chrome 120+ configureWorld, Chrome 135+ execute). The USER_SCRIPT world is exempt from page CSP and supports configureWorld({ csp: "script-src 'self' 'unsafe-eval'" }) to allow eval. This is the same approach Violentmonkey and Tampermonkey plan for MV3. Requires adding "userScripts" permission and user must enable "Allow User Scripts" toggle.

See attached eval-csp-research.md for full analysis, Chromium source investigation, comparison of Violentmonkey/Tampermonkey approaches, and alternative solutions considered.

examples.text: Agent executes 'document.title' and receives the actual page title instead of null
Agent executes '1 + 1' and receives '2'
Agent executes invalid JS like 'throw new Error("test")' and receives an MCP error result with the error message
When userScripts API is unavailable, agent receives an error explaining how to enable it (toggle 'Allow User Scripts')
Service worker startup calls configureWorld to set permissive CSP for USER_SCRIPT world
manifest.json includes userScripts permission

rules.text: chrome.scripting.executeScript with eval() is blocked by MV3 CSP in the extension's ISOLATED world — eval() silently returns null
chrome.userScripts API (Chrome 120+ configureWorld, Chrome 135+ execute) provides a USER_SCRIPT world exempt from page CSP and configurable with custom CSP
userScripts permission and configureWorld() must be called on service worker startup before any script execution
When userScripts API is unavailable (user hasn't enabled toggle), the handler must return a clear error message explaining the requirement
The USER_SCRIPT world CSP must include 'unsafe-eval' and 'unsafe-inline' to allow eval() and dynamic code execution
Script execution errors must be caught and returned as MCP error results, not silently swallowed

EXT-010.title: browser_execute_script returns null — eval() blocked by CSP in extension isolated world

userStory.action: execute arbitrary JavaScript in a browser tab via browser_execute_script
userStory.benefit: I can extract data, check state, and manipulate the DOM beyond what specialized tools offer

architectureNotes.text: Uses chrome.tabs.create() API. Chromium C++ implementation: TabsCreateFunction in chrome/browser/extensions/api/tabs/tabs_api.h. API schema: chrome/common/extensions/api/tabs.json. Helper: ExtensionTabUtil::OpenTab in chrome/browser/extensions/extension_tab_util.h.
Changes in 2 files only: extension/src/background/browser-tools.ts (handler + interface) and extension/host/lib/mcp-server.mjs (NATIVE_TOOLS entry). Plus docs: extension/webmcp-skill.md.

EXT-011.description:
The extension exposes 11 native browser control tools but is missing the ability to CREATE new tabs. It can close tabs (browser_close_tab), switch tabs (browser_switch_tab), list tabs (browser_list_tabs), and navigate existing tabs (browser_navigate) — but there is no way for the AI agent to open a URL in a new tab.

The workaround of using browser_execute_script with window.open() fails because Chrome's popup blocker blocks it (no user gesture context in the USER_SCRIPT world).

This is a clear gap: the agent can close and manage tabs but cannot create them.

Fix: Add a browser_create_tab tool that calls chrome.tabs.create(). This requires changes in two places:
1. extension/src/background/browser-tools.ts — add handler + extend ChromeTabsForTools interface with create()
2. extension/host/lib/mcp-server.mjs — add tool definition to NATIVE_TOOLS array

The chrome.tabs.create() API requires NO additional permissions beyond what the extension already has (the 'tabs' permission is already declared in manifest.json). Per Chrome docs: 'creating a new tab' does not require any permissions.

examples.text: Agent calls browser_create_tab with {url: 'https://example.com'} → new tab opens, navigates to URL, returns {tabId, url, title, active: true, windowId}
Agent calls browser_create_tab with no arguments → new blank tab opens (chrome://newtab), returns immediately with {tabId, url: '', title: '', active: true}
Agent calls browser_create_tab with {url: 'https://example.com', active: false} → tab opens in background, returns {active: false}
Agent calls browser_create_tab with {url: 'https://example.com', pinned: true} → pinned tab created
Tool appears in tools/list response as 12th native tool alongside existing 11

rules.text: chrome.tabs.create() requires NO additional permissions - creating a tab is permission-free per Chrome docs
The handler must add 'create' to the ChromeTabsForTools interface for dependency injection
