architectureNotes.text: Multi-phase scan: (1) getAllFrames discovers frames, (2) main frame scanPageDOM detects <iframe> elements and records their position/depth, (3) per-frame executeScript with frameIds runs scanPageDOM in each iframe, (4) service worker merges results — main frame tree + iframe subtrees spliced at the correct positions. Refs assigned per-frame with f{frameId}e{N} prefix for non-main frames. RefEntry gains frameId field so click/fill targets the right frame.

getAllFrames() returns MORE fields than documented in research: per Chromium IDL (web_navigation.json), each frame object includes: errorOccurred (boolean), processId (integer), frameId (integer), parentFrameId (integer), url (string), documentId (string), parentDocumentId (string, optional), documentLifecycle (enum: prerender/active/cached/pending_deletion), frameType (enum: outermost_frame/fenced_frame/sub_frame). The documentId and frameType fields are particularly useful — documentId enables precise correlation with InjectionResult.documentId, and frameType distinguishes sub_frame from the main frame without relying on frameId===0.

Chrome 133+ behavior change: Since Chrome 133, chrome.scripting.executeScript uses match_origin_as_fallback by default (PSA from Chrome Extensions DevRel, Jan 2025). This means executeScript now injects into MORE frames by default, including about:blank and sandboxed srcdoc frames that previously required explicit match_origin_as_fallback. This improves iframe scanning coverage automatically. Source: groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/chromium-extensions/c/D8DcJARVM90

LOCATE-009.description:
Extend browser_scan_page, browser_click_element, browser_fill_form, and browser_diff_page to discover and interact with elements inside iframes. Currently all scanning is scoped to the top-level frame only — elements inside same-origin and cross-origin iframes are invisible to the AI agent.

Chrome's chrome.scripting.executeScript API supports targeting specific frames via frameIds and discovering all frames in a tab via chrome.webNavigation.getAllFrames(). Same-origin iframes can also be scanned by the top-level injection walking into contentDocument. Cross-origin iframes require separate executeScript calls per frameId.

The scan output should nest iframe content under the iframe element in the accessibility tree, with refs that encode the frameId so click/fill can target the correct frame. Example: refs like 'f2e5' meaning frame 2, element 5.

examples.text: Page with Stripe payment iframe: scan returns main frame elements (e1, e2) plus iframe content as nested children (f5e1 'Card Number', f5e2 'Expiry', f5e3 'CVC', f5e4 'Pay'). AI fills card fields using @f5e1, @f5e2, @f5e3 and clicks @f5e4.
Page with no iframes: scan returns only main frame elements with simple refs (e1, e2, e3) — 100% backward compatible, no behavioral change
Click on iframe element using @f5e4: resolveRefSelector parses 'f5e4' → frameId=5, elementRef='e4', looks up CSS selector, then executeScript targets frameIds: [5] to click within the iframe
Ad-heavy page with 25 iframes: maxFrames=10 limits scanning to the 10 largest/most relevant frames, remaining iframes show as 'iframe [skipped]' in the tree

Nested iframes (iframe inside iframe): getAllFrames returns all frames at all depths with parentFrameId chain. Tree shows nested indentation correctly. Refs use the direct frame's ID (f12e1), not the parent chain

Sandboxed iframe with sandbox='allow-same-origin' (no allow-scripts): executeScript in ISOLATED world still succeeds — scanPageDOM runs and returns elements. The iframe appears in tree with its content. The sandbox attribute only blocks MAIN world scripts, not extension content scripts.

rules.text: manifest.json must include 'webNavigation' permission to enable chrome.webNavigation.getAllFrames() for frame discovery
Frame discovery uses chrome.webNavigation.getAllFrames() to enumerate all frames in a tab — returns frameId, parentFrameId, url for each frame including nested iframes
chrome.scripting.executeScript with frameIds targets specific frames — works for both same-origin AND cross-origin iframes because the extension has <all_urls> host permission
Main frame refs remain backward-compatible (e1, e2, e3). Iframe refs use frame-prefixed format: f{frameId}e{N} (e.g. f5e1 = frame 5, element 1). The @ prefix works for both: @e1 and @f5e3
RefEntry must gain a frameId field (0 for main frame) so click/fill can target the correct frame via chrome.scripting.executeScript({ target: { tabId, frameIds: [frameId] } })
Iframe content appears nested under the iframe element in the accessibility tree output — the tree shows the iframe's src/name, then indented children from the frame scan
A maxFrames parameter (default 10) limits the number of iframes scanned to prevent timeout on ad-heavy pages. Same-origin and larger iframes are prioritized over small cross-origin ones
browser_diff_page must produce diffs on the merged multi-frame tree. Frame additions/removals (iframes dynamically created or destroyed) appear as tree-level changes

CRITICAL CORRECTION (from Chromium source review): Sandboxed iframes WITHOUT allow-scripts CAN be scanned via chrome.scripting.executeScript in ISOLATED world (the default). The sandbox attribute only blocks MAIN world scripts. Extension content scripts in ISOLATED world bypass sandbox restrictions. This was confirmed by Chromium bug 355256366 (fixed Chrome 130) and the Chrome 133 PSA that made match_origin_as_fallback the default for executeScript. Rule [6] claim about sandbox-no-scripts skipping is WRONG for our use case.

Non-scannable frames must be skipped gracefully: chrome-extension:// and chrome:// URLs. about:blank frames should be scanned if they have content (same-origin JS-populated). about:srcdoc frames (url='about:srcdoc') should always be scanned. Sandboxed iframes WITHOUT allow-scripts CAN still be scanned because executeScript runs in ISOLATED world which bypasses sandbox script restrictions (only MAIN world is blocked). The iframe element always appears in the tree regardless.

Frame-to-DOM correlation uses a two-pass injection approach: (1) First pass: inject a marker into each frame via executeScript({ frameIds: [fid], func: (id) => { window.__fspec_frameId = id; }, args: [fid] }), setting a global variable with the frameId. (2) Second pass: parent frame scan detects all <iframe> elements. For same-origin iframes, reads iframe.contentWindow.__fspec_frameId for exact frameId→DOM mapping. For cross-origin iframes (where contentWindow access is blocked by SOP), falls back to matching iframe.src against getAllFrames().url — cross-origin duplicates with identical URLs are rare and use document order as tiebreaker.

architectureNotes.text: Three-Layer Lock Architecture: Layer 1 (Inter-Process) = proper-lockfile with mkdir strategy for cross-process coordination; Layer 2 (In-Process) = Readers-writer pattern using promises and queues for concurrent reads; Layer 3 (Atomic Writes) = Temp file + rename for POSIX atomic write guarantees

LockedFileManager Singleton Pattern: Single instance coordinates all in-process locks via Map<string, number> for read counts and Set<string> for write locks, with separate waiting queues (Array<() => void>) for blocked readers and writers

proper-lockfile Configuration: stale=10000ms (10 second timeout for crashed processes), retries={retries:10, minTimeout:50ms, maxTimeout:500ms} for exponential backoff, realpath=false for symlink support and performance
Affected Files: work-units.json (230+ work units, high contention), foundation.json, tags.json, prefixes.json, epics.json, example-map.json, fspec-hooks.json - ALL must use LockedFileManager

examples.text: User runs 'fspec list-work-units' in terminal 1 AND 'fspec update-work-unit-status BOARD-001 done' in terminal 2 simultaneously - Both commands acquire proper-lockfile locks, list-work-units reads while update-work-unit-status waits for write lock, no corruption occurs

TUI board is running (refreshing every 2 seconds) AND user runs 'fspec create-story PREFIX Title' - TUI's read lock and command's write lock coordinate via proper-lockfile, work-units.json is never corrupted, TUI sees new work unit after refresh

Three fspec commands run concurrently: (1) list-work-units, (2) show-work-unit BOARD-001, (3) update-work-unit-status BOARD-002 done - Commands 1 and 2 read concurrently with in-process readers lock, command 3 waits for exclusive write lock, all succeed without corruption

Process 1 acquires write lock on work-units.json and crashes mid-write - proper-lockfile's stale lock detection (10 second timeout) allows Process 2 to acquire lock after timeout, preventing permanent deadlock

Command writes to work-units.json using atomic pattern: (1) writes to work-units.json.tmp.abc123, (2) renames to work-units.json - If crash occurs during step 1, original file is intact; if during step 2, rename is atomic

Reader 1 and Reader 2 both call fileManager.readJSON('work-units.json') - Both acquire in-process read locks simultaneously (readers-writer pattern), both acquire proper-lockfile locks with retry, both read file concurrently

Writer calls fileManager.writeJSON('work-units.json', data) while Reader is active - Writer waits for Reader's in-process read lock to release, then acquires exclusive write lock, prevents read-during-write corruption

Command refactoring minimal change: Replace 'const data = await ensureWorkUnitsFile(cwd); ... await writeFile(file, JSON.stringify(data, 2))' with 'await fileManager.transaction(file, async (data) => { ... })' - same 400 lines of mutation logic unchanged

Transaction rollback on error: 'await fileManager.transaction(file, async (data) => { if (\!valid) throw new Error("bad"); data.x = 1; })' - Error thrown, no write occurs, file unchanged, error propagates to command catch block

Multi-file sequential transactions: 'await fileManager.transaction(workUnitsFile, async (data) => { data.workUnits[id] = newWorkUnit; }); await fileManager.transaction(epicsFile, async (data) => { data.epics[epicId].workUnits.push(id); });' - If second fails first committed, run fspec repair-work-units to fix

rules.text: File locking MUST use three-layer architecture: (1) proper-lockfile for inter-process coordination, (2) readers-writer pattern for in-process optimization, (3) atomic write-replace for safe writes
Multiple readers can read the same file concurrently (readers-writer pattern allows parallel reads)
Only ONE writer can modify a file at a time (exclusive write lock blocks all readers and other writers)
All file writes MUST use atomic write-replace pattern (write to temp file + rename) to prevent partial writes
proper-lockfile MUST use stale lock detection (10 second timeout) to prevent deadlocks from crashed processes
Lock acquisition MUST use retry logic with exponential backoff (10 retries, 50-500ms timeout range)
LockedFileManager MUST be a singleton to ensure in-process lock coordination across all file operations
All JSON file operations (work-units.json, tags.json, foundation.json, etc.) MUST use LockedFileManager
Read-modify-write operations MUST use transaction() method to ensure atomicity of the entire operation
Lock release MUST happen in finally block to prevent lock leaks on errors

YES - Support network filesystems. proper-lockfile's mkdir strategy is atomic on both local and network filesystems (NFS, SMB). No additional implementation cost, works in CI/CD and team environments.

Throw error immediately after 10 retries with exponential backoff (50-500ms, ~5 seconds total). Simple, clean error message: 'Failed to acquire file lock. Check for stuck fspec processes.' Exit code 1.

NEVER cache file contents. Always read from disk for consistency. Files are small (~200KB max), reads are fast (~3-5ms), caching adds complexity and risk of stale data across processes. Correctness > speed.

Optional debug metrics via FSPEC_DEBUG_LOCKS environment variable. Logs lock acquisition time, wait time, retries, hold duration. Ties into LOG-001 logging infrastructure. Silent by default, verbose when debugging.

All-at-once migration (NOT incremental). MUST work 100% perfectly the first time. Complete implementation: LockedFileManager + refactor utilities + refactor all ~50 commands + refactor TUI store + comprehensive tests. No partial states, no gradual rollout.
ensure* functions use read-lock-first pattern: attempt read with READ lock, on ENOENT upgrade to WRITE lock with double-check before creating file
READ locks released immediately after JSON.parse() completes - data is in memory, lock no longer needed, allows other operations to proceed
transaction() method uses mutation-based API: callback receives data, mutates in place, returns void - fileManager writes mutated data automatically on completion
transaction() errors cause rollback: if callback throws error, no write occurs and file remains unchanged - error propagates to caller for proper logging and exit codes

Multi-file operations use sequential transactions (not atomic): each file gets separate transaction, if later transaction fails earlier transactions already committed - acceptable due to denormalized data, defensive querying, and repair utilities

Debug metrics enabled via FSPEC_DEBUG_LOCKS environment variable: logs lock type, file path, wait time, hold duration, retry count - silent by default, verbose when debugging - ties into LOG-001 logging infrastructure when available

architectureNotes.text: ConnectMCP tool uses rmcp crate (same as Codex) for MCP JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio transport (TokioChildProcess) and Streamable HTTP transport (StreamableHttpClientTransport). Protocol version: 2025-11-25

MCP lifecycle per connection: spawn/connect → initialize handshake (protocolVersion, capabilities, clientInfo/serverInfo) → notifications/initialized → tools/list → cache tools on session. MCP spec 2025-11-25 section: Lifecycle

Tool routing: mcp__<server>__<tool>(args) → split on '__' → lookup server in session.mcp_connections → send JSON-RPC {method: 'tools/call', params: {name: '<tool>', arguments: args}} → return content array from response

Server-initiated messages handled via rmcp ClientHandler trait: notifications/tools/list_changed → re-fetch tools/list + inject notification; notifications/resources/updated → inject notification; sampling/createMessage → inject into session via watcher_input_tx, route LLM response back as sampling result

Ephemeral session state: session.mcp_connections: HashMap<String, McpConnection> where McpConnection holds RmcpClient, cached Vec<Tool> from tools/list, server InitializeResult, optional child PID. Tool list assembled fresh each LLM call: built_in_tools + mcp_connections.flat_map(tools)

rmcp API: handler.serve(transport) does full initialize handshake (sends InitializeRequest with ClientInfo, receives ServerInfo, sends InitializedNotification). Returns RunningService<RoleClient, H> where peer() provides list_all_tools(), call_tool(), list_all_resources(), etc. ClientHandler trait has on_tool_list_changed, on_resource_updated, create_message, on_logging_message callbacks

The sampling/createMessage round-trip uses a dedicated oneshot channel: create_message handler creates oneshot pair, injects SamplingRequest(params, oneshot_tx) via watcher_input_tx, the agent_loop processes it as a special WatcherInput variant that captures the LLM response and sends it through oneshot_tx, handler awaits oneshot_rx and returns CreateMessageResult to rmcp

MCP tools are injected into the LLM via a generic McpToolWrapper that implements rig::tool::Tool trait. Each provider's create_rig_agent() accepts an optional Vec<McpToolWrapper> parameter and appends them to the agent builder. Since create_rig_agent() is called fresh each turn inside agent_loop, newly connected MCP tools appear immediately in the next turn

MCP-001.description: Implement Dynamic MCP — an architecture where MCP server connections are established through a ConnectMCP tool call at runtime, rather than static config files at session startup. The agent decides when to connect, receives structured feedback on success or failure, and gains typed MCP tools dynamically mid-session. Uses the rmcp crate for native MCP protocol handling. Server-initiated messages (notifications, sampling requests) are injected into the session via watcher_input_tx. Skills can describe ConnectMCP calls, enabling multi-server workflows that are impossible with static MCP (Codex, OpenCode).

examples.text: Agent calls ConnectMCP(name: 'github', transport: 'stdio', command: 'npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-github') → tool spawns child process, sends JSON-RPC initialize request (protocolVersion: '2025-11-25', capabilities, clientInfo), receives server capabilities with tools: {listChanged: true}, sends notifications/initialized, then calls tools/list → caches tool definitions (name, description, inputSchema per MCP spec) → returns structured result to LLM listing server name, protocol version, and discovered tools

LLM calls mcp__github__create_issue({owner: 'org', repo: 'project', title: 'Bug fix'}) → tool routes to cached github connection → sends JSON-RPC tools/call with {name: 'create_issue', arguments: {...}} → MCP server returns {content: [{type: 'text', text: 'Created issue #42'}], isError: false} → tool returns content to LLM as tool result

ConnectMCP(name: 'db', transport: 'stdio', command: 'python3 db-mcp-server.py') fails because python3 is not installed → tool catches spawn error and returns structured failure to LLM with stderr output → LLM can reason about the failure and suggest 'python3 is not installed, try: brew install python3'

Skill file describes two ConnectMCP calls (github stdio server + sonarqube HTTP server) → agent executes skill, connects both mid-session → tools/list from each server returns tool definitions with inputSchema → agent now has typed tools from both servers (mcp__github__*, mcp__sonar__*) and uses them in a multi-server workflow → session ends, both child processes killed

Connected MCP server sends JSON-RPC notification {method: 'notifications/tools/list_changed'} → ClientHandler callback fires → tool re-calls tools/list to refresh cached tool definitions → injects '[MCP:github] Server tools list changed — refreshed 5 tools' into session via watcher_input_tx → next LLM API call includes updated tool schemas

MCP server sends sampling/createMessage request with {messages: [{role: 'user', content: {type: 'text', text: 'Analyze this code...'}}], maxTokens: 500} → injected into session as input for the LLM to process → LLM response routed back through the connection as the sampling result

Agent calls ConnectMCP(action: 'list') → returns 'Connected MCP servers: github — connected 5m ago, 5 tools, 12 calls; sonar — connected 2m ago, 3 tools, 0 calls' → Agent calls ConnectMCP(action: 'disconnect', name: 'github') → connection closed, child process killed → returns '✓ Disconnected: github (was connected 5m, 12 tool calls made)' → mcp__github__* tools removed from next LLM turn

ConnectMCP(name: 'slow-server', transport: 'stdio', command: 'node slow-mcp.js', timeout: 5) → server starts but does not respond to initialize within 5 seconds → tool kills the process and returns structured error: '✗ Failed to connect: slow-server — Timeout: MCP handshake not completed within 5s. Process started (PID 48291) but did not respond.' → LLM can reason about the timeout and suggest increasing it or checking the server

rules.text: ConnectMCP is a tool call — the agent calls it to establish MCP server connections at runtime (Dynamic MCP), not through config files at startup (Static MCP)
ConnectMCP uses the rmcp crate to speak native MCP JSON-RPC — it spawns the server process (stdio) or opens HTTP connection, performs the initialization handshake, and calls tools/list

On success, ConnectMCP returns a structured tool result listing the server name, protocol version, and all discovered tools with their schemas — these tools then become callable as mcp__<server>__<tool> in subsequent LLM turns
On failure, ConnectMCP returns a structured error (runtime not found, handshake timeout, auth required) so the LLM can reason about it, suggest fixes, or try alternatives
MCP connections are ephemeral — cached on the session as a HashMap<String, McpConnection>, gathered fresh each LLM API call, no persistent registry or lifecycle manager
Server-initiated MCP messages (notifications, sampling requests, resource updates) are injected into the session via watcher_input_tx so the LLM sees them
MCP tool calls (mcp__<server>__<tool>) are routed through the cached connection — look up server in session.mcp_connections, forward via client.call_tool()
Connection lifecycle is tied to the session — when session ends, all McpConnections are dropped and child processes killed
Skills can describe ConnectMCP calls inline — enabling multi-server workflows where the agent connects to each MCP server as needed during skill execution
ConnectMCP tool call — agent decides when to connect dynamically. No auto-start, no config files.

For sampling/createMessage: inject as session input, LLM responds, response returned via the rmcp ClientHandler. The MCP spec defines this as a server→client request — our ClientHandler impl handles the round-trip natively.

ConnectMCP calls tools/list during initialization and returns the discovered tools to the LLM. Server capabilities are negotiated during the initialize handshake. No separate manifest needed — the MCP protocol handles discovery natively.

ConnectMCP supports three actions: connect (default — establish new server connection), disconnect (tear down named connection, kill child process), and list (show all active connections with tool counts and uptime)

ConnectMCP enforces a configurable timeout (default 10 seconds) for the initialization handshake — if the server does not complete initialize within the timeout, the process is killed and a structured timeout error is returned to the LLM
Config file support for pre-declaring MCP servers is V2 scope — the agent would read a config and call ConnectMCP for each entry. V1 has no config file; all connections are explicit tool calls
MCP tool names are namespaced as mcp__<server>__<tool> — the double-underscore prevents collisions between servers that expose tools with the same name, and between MCP tools and built-in tools

ConnectMCP connect action accepts optional env (HashMap<String,String>) for stdio transport passed to Command::envs(), and optional headers (HashMap<String,String>) for HTTP transport passed to StreamableHttpClientTransport. These enable passing API tokens, credentials, and auth headers to MCP servers

architectureNotes.text: File structure: src/migrations/ with index.ts (runner), registry.ts (version tracking), types.ts (interfaces), migrations/ subfolder for individual migration files, __tests__/ for tests
Migration interface: {version: string, name: string, description: string, up: (data) => data, down?: (data) => data}. Each migration has unique version number.
Registry pattern: migrations array in registry.ts exports all migrations in version order. getMigrationsToApply(currentVersion, targetVersion) returns migrations to run.
Auto-migration integration: ensureWorkUnitsFile() in src/utils/ensure-files.ts calls ensureLatestVersion(cwd, CURRENT_VERSION) before returning data
Backup naming: work-units.json.backup-{version}-{timestamp} (e.g., work-units.json.backup-0.7.0-1738329600000). Stored in same directory as work-units.json.
Version comparison: Use semver-compatible compareVersions(v1, v2) function. Returns -1 (v1 < v2), 0 (equal), or 1 (v1 > v2).
Migration history structure in work-units.json: migrationHistory: [{version: '0.7.0', applied: '2025-01-31T12:00:00Z', backupPath: 'spec/work-units.json.backup-0.7.0-1738329600000'}]
Error handling: Migration failure throws error with migration version, does NOT automatically restore backup. User can manually restore from backup file if needed.
Console output: Use chalk.yellow for warnings, chalk.blue for migration names, chalk.green for success, chalk.red for errors, chalk.dim for backup paths. Show progress for each migration.
Transaction safety: Each migration runs atomically - backup created first, then migration up() called, then data saved. If up() throws, data is not saved.
Version field location: Add 'version' field at root level of work-units.json (same level as 'workUnits' and 'states'). Default to undefined for old files (treated as v0.6.0).
Manual command structure: 'fspec migrate' with options: --version X.Y.Z (migrate to specific version), --status (show migration info), --rollback (undo last migration if down() exists)

assumptions: Support optional down() function for rollback, but not required for all migrations. Document as 'probably not needed' for most cases.

Tool call ID linkage: After resume, tool_result messages are correctly linked to their tool_call messages via matching IDs, so LLM can trace which result corresponds to which call.
Context continuation: User asks 'what else was in that file?' after resume. LLM can answer because it has the full tool result content, not just summary text.
Turn boundary restoration: Session had 10 user-assistant exchanges. After resume, session.turns has 10 entries so compaction can summarize by turn boundaries.
Image in conversation: User pastes screenshot, assistant analyzes it. After resume, the actual image data is restored from blob storage, not just a broken URL reference.

PROV-012.description:
Implement the full Anthropic OAuth login flow so users with Claude Max/Pro subscriptions can authenticate directly from codelet, rather than requiring CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN to be manually set.

Currently we support CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN env var for OAuth mode (claude.rs). This story adds the actual login flow:

1. **PKCE OAuth authorization** - Redirect to claude.ai/oauth/authorize (Max) or console.anthropic.com/oauth/authorize (Console) with PKCE challenge
2. **Manual code entry** - User pastes authorization code from browser callback page
3. **Token exchange** - POST to console.anthropic.com/v1/oauth/token with authorization_code grant
4. **Token refresh** - Refresh expired access tokens using refresh_token grant  
5. **API key creation** - Option to create API key via console.anthropic.com/api/oauth/claude_cli/create_api_key
6. **Request modifications for OAuth mode**:
   - Authorization: Bearer header (instead of x-api-key)
   - anthropic-beta: oauth-2025-04-20,interleaved-thinking-2025-05-14
   - user-agent: claude-cli/2.1.3 (external, cli)
   - Tool name prefixing with mcp_ prefix (and stripping on response)
   - URL modification: ?beta=true query parameter
   - System prompt: Replace app name with 'Claude Code' in system blocks
7. **Credential persistence** - Store refresh/access tokens securely (keyring or encrypted file)
8. **TUI integration** - Add OAuth login option to provider settings

Reference implementations:
- /tmp/anthropic-auth-inspect/package/index.mjs (opencode's Anthropic auth plugin - full PKCE + code exchange flow)
- /tmp/opencode/packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/auth.ts (CLI auth command flow)
- /tmp/opencode/packages/opencode/src/provider/auth.ts (provider auth abstraction)

PROV-013.description:
Implement the local HTTP server on port 1455 that handles the OAuth callback during browser-based PKCE login.

All OAuth logic already exists in Rust (codex_oauth.rs + codex_auth.rs). This card adds the missing piece: a hyper-based HTTP server in codelet/providers/src/codex/codex_oauth_server.rs that binds to port 1455 and orchestrates the flow.

The server:
1. Binds to port 1455 using hyper
2. Generates PKCE + state (codex_oauth.rs generate_pkce/generate_state)
3. Opens browser to authorize URL (open crate + codex_oauth.rs build_authorize_url)
4. Waits for callback with 5-min timeout (OAuthTimeout)
5. Validates state (validate_oauth_callback)
6. Exchanges code for tokens via reqwest POST to issuer/oauth/token (new exchange_authorization_code fn)
7. Extracts account_id from JWT (extract_account_id)
8. Persists tokens to auth.json (write_codex_auth)
9. Returns CodexTokens to caller

Routes: /auth/callback (main), /cancel (abort), 404 for everything else.

Entire flow stays in Rust - no NAPI round-trips needed. Single public entry point: async fn browser_oauth_login() -> Result<CodexTokens>.

PROV-014.description:
Implement the device auth flow for environments where a browser can't be opened (SSH, containers, headless servers).

OpenCode's device auth pattern:
1. POST to {ISSUER}/api/accounts/deviceauth/usercode with client_id → get device_auth_id + user_code + interval
2. Display user_code and URL ({ISSUER}/codex/device) to the user
3. Poll {ISSUER}/api/accounts/deviceauth/token at the specified interval
4. When user completes auth on external device, endpoint returns authorization_code + code_verifier
5. Exchange authorization_code for tokens via {ISSUER}/oauth/token (grant_type=authorization_code)
6. Persist tokens to auth.json

This is the headless alternative to the browser OAuth server flow (PROV-013). Both flows produce the same CodexTokens output.

User sees 'Enter code ABCD-1234 at https://auth.openai.com/codex/device'. Polling starts. After user authorizes on phone, poll returns authorization_code and code_verifier. Code exchanged for tokens. Tokens persisted to auth.json.
Polling receives authorization_pending status: system waits for the specified interval (e.g. 5 seconds) and polls again without error
Polling receives expired_token error: device code has expired (user took too long), flow terminates with clear error message
Polling receives access_denied error: user explicitly denied authorization, flow terminates with clear error message
Device auth flow times out: user never authorizes, overall timeout (e.g. 15 minutes) expires, flow terminates gracefully
Usercode endpoint returns error (network failure): flow terminates immediately with descriptive error, no polling attempted
Token exchange after device auth succeeds: authorization_code + code_verifier exchanged at /oauth/token with grant_type=authorization_code, returns tokens including id_token with account_id claim
Device auth output matches browser OAuth: both flows produce identical CodexTokens struct with id_token, access_token, refresh_token, account_id
Polling receives slow_down response: system increases polling interval by 5 seconds (e.g. 5s becomes 10s) and continues polling

PROV-015.description:
Expose the Rust OAuth flows (browser login + device auth) to the TypeScript TUI layer via NAPI bindings.

OpenCode's architecture: The codex.ts plugin runs entirely in JS/Bun. Codelet's architecture is different — the OAuth logic lives in Rust (codelet-providers), and the TUI is TypeScript/Ink. The bridge is NAPI.

Needed NAPI functions:
1. codex_oauth_browser_login() → starts the hyper server (PROV-013), opens browser, returns a Promise that resolves with serialized tokens when callback completes or rejects on timeout/error
2. codex_oauth_device_login() → initiates device auth (PROV-014), returns { user_code, verification_url, promise } where promise resolves with tokens when polling completes
3. codex_oauth_refresh_token(refresh_token: string) → refreshes access token, returns new tokens
4. codex_oauth_get_tokens() → reads current tokens from auth.json (or returns null if none exist)

These are async NAPI functions that spawn tokio tasks internally.

examples.text: TUI calls codex_oauth_browser_login(): tokio spawns browser_oauth_login(), browser opens, user authorizes, Promise resolves with NapiCodexTokens containing id_token, access_token, refresh_token, account_id

TUI calls codex_oauth_device_login(): Rust calls request_device_code(), returns NapiDeviceAuthStartResult with user_code='ABCD-1234' and verification_url='https://auth.openai.com/codex/device'. TUI displays these. Background promise polls and resolves with NapiCodexTokens when user completes auth

TUI calls codex_oauth_refresh_token('rt_abc123'): Rust calls refresh_access_token(), returns NapiCodexTokens with refreshed access_token. Also persists updated tokens to auth.json and extracts account_id from the new id_token
TUI calls codex_oauth_get_tokens() with valid auth.json: returns NapiCodexTokens with all 4 fields populated from the stored tokens
TUI calls codex_oauth_get_tokens() with no auth.json: returns null (not an error — absence of tokens is a valid state)
Browser login times out: codex_oauth_browser_login() Promise rejects with descriptive error 'OAuth login timed out after 300 seconds'
Device auth polling fails with expired_token: Promise rejects with error 'Device auth failed: Device code has expired...'
Token refresh fails (invalid refresh_token): codex_oauth_refresh_token() Promise rejects with error describing the failure status

rules.text: codex_oauth_browser_login() is an async NAPI function that spawns a tokio task to run browser_oauth_login(), returning a Promise<NapiCodexTokens> to TypeScript
codex_oauth_device_login() is an async NAPI function that returns NapiDeviceAuthStartResult with user_code, verification_url, and a Promise<NapiCodexTokens> that resolves when polling completes
codex_oauth_refresh_token(refresh_token: string) is an async NAPI function that calls refresh_access_token() and returns refreshed NapiCodexTokens
codex_oauth_get_tokens() is a synchronous NAPI function that reads auth.json via read_codex_auth() and returns NapiCodexTokens or null
All NAPI functions convert Rust errors to napi::Error via Error::from_reason() — TypeScript sees rejected promises with descriptive error messages
NapiCodexTokens is an #[napi(object)] struct with fields: id_token, access_token, refresh_token, account_id — all strings, matching the Rust CodexTokens struct

Device auth NAPI binding needs a two-phase design: first returns user_code and verification_url synchronously (so TUI can display them), then provides a promise that resolves when the polling completes
The NAPI module file is codelet/napi/src/codex_oauth.rs, registered in lib.rs under #[cfg(not(feature = "noop"))]

architectureNotes.text: New file: codelet/providers/src/codex/refreshing_client.rs — Implements RefreshingCodexClient struct that wraps reqwest::Client and implements rig's HttpClientExt trait. Contains TokenState struct with access_token, refresh_token, account_id, and expires_at (Instant). Arc<RwLock<TokenState>> for shared mutable state.

refresh_access_token_at() from codex_oauth.rs is the refresh function used — it takes an issuer URL (testable with wiremock) and returns TokenRefreshResponse with expires_in. The RefreshingCodexClient stores the issuer URL for testability.

The rig CompletionsClient builder accepts the generic H via ClientBuilder<OpenAICompletionsExtBuilder, OpenAIApiKey, H> — we pass RefreshingCodexClient as H. The builder's .api_key() sets a dummy key (RefreshingCodexClient replaces it). No .base_url() needed since RefreshingCodexClient rewrites URLs itself.

CodexProvider struct is UNIFIED: both OAuth and API key modes use RefreshingCodexClient. Fields become CompletionModel<RefreshingCodexClient> and CompletionsClient<RefreshingCodexClient>. RefreshingCodexClient has an internal TokenMode enum: OAuth{token_state, issuer_url} for refresh+rewrite+headers, ApiKey for pass-through to reqwest. No enum wrapper or generics needed on CodexProvider itself.

assumptions: The existing from_oauth_tokens() static headers approach is INCOMPATIBLE with token refresh — once rig builds the client, headers can't change. The RefreshingCodexClient solves this by intercepting at the HTTP layer where it can dynamically set headers on every request.
Token expiry uses a 30-second buffer (refresh when expires_at - 30s < now) to prevent edge cases where token expires between check and actual API call
PROV-016.description:
Implement the custom fetch/HTTP middleware layer that intercepts Codex API requests to:
1. Auto-refresh expired access tokens before each request
2. Rewrite URLs from standard OpenAI endpoints to chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses
3. Replace the Authorization header with Bearer {access_token}
4. Add ChatGPT-Account-Id header
5. Add originator header

In OpenCode, this is done via a custom `fetch` function returned by the auth loader plugin (codex.ts lines 417-494). The fetch function:
- Strips the dummy API key authorization header
- Checks if token is expired, refreshes if needed using refreshAccessToken()
- Builds new headers with Bearer token + account ID
- Rewrites URL if path includes /v1/responses or /chat/completions
- Calls the real fetch with modified request

In codelet, this lives in the Rust provider layer. The from_oauth_tokens() constructor already sets base_url and headers via rig's client builder, but it doesn't handle:
- Runtime token refresh (token could expire mid-session)
- Dynamic header updates after refresh

Options: (a) wrap the reqwest client with a middleware layer, (b) check-and-refresh before each completion call in CodexProvider, or (c) use a RefreshingClient wrapper pattern.

examples.text: Token still valid: CodexProvider makes API call, RefreshingCodexClient checks expiry (30 min remaining), skips refresh, rewrites URL to CODEX_API_ENDPOINT, sets Bearer + account headers, forwards to reqwest

Token expired mid-session: CodexProvider makes API call, RefreshingCodexClient detects expiry, calls refresh_access_token_at() with stored refresh_token, gets new tokens, persists to auth.json, updates in-memory state, retries original request with fresh token
Token refresh fails (invalid refresh_token): RefreshingCodexClient attempts refresh, gets 401, returns error to CodexProvider without sending original request — user sees auth error
URL with no rewrite needed (e.g. /v1/models): RefreshingCodexClient passes URL through unchanged but still sets auth headers
Streaming request with expired token: RefreshingCodexClient refreshes token before forwarding the streaming request, SSE stream works with fresh credentials
Concurrent requests during refresh: Two requests arrive while token is expired, only one refresh occurs (RwLock ensures serialization), both requests proceed with the same refreshed token
CodexProvider::from_oauth_tokens() integration: constructs RefreshingCodexClient with initial tokens, passes as generic H to CompletionsClient builder, provider methods use it transparently

URL rewrite for /v1/responses: rig sends request to https://api.openai.com/v1/responses (default OpenAI base URL), RefreshingCodexClient detects /v1/responses in URL, rewrites to https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses
Token refresh response has no expires_in field: RefreshingCodexClient defaults to 3600 seconds (1 hour), applies 30s buffer, next refresh triggers at 3570 seconds

API key mode pass-through: CodexProvider::from_api_key() creates RefreshingCodexClient in ApiKey mode, requests flow through to reqwest unchanged — no URL rewrite, no token refresh, no header injection

rules.text: Implement HttpClientExt trait for a RefreshingCodexClient that wraps reqwest::Client, intercepting every HTTP request to check token expiry, refresh if needed, rewrite URL, and set headers
Token expiry is tracked using expires_in from TokenRefreshResponse — if current time >= stored expiry, refresh before the request
Token refresh uses existing refresh_access_token() from codex_oauth.rs with the stored refresh_token
After refresh, updated tokens (access_token, refresh_token, id_token) are persisted to auth.json via write_codex_auth() and the in-memory state is updated
URL rewriting uses existing rewrite_codex_url() — URLs containing /v1/responses or /chat/completions are rewritten to CODEX_API_ENDPOINT
Every request sets three headers: Authorization (Bearer {access_token}), ChatGPT-Account-Id ({account_id}), originator (codelet)
CodexProvider::from_oauth_tokens() changes from building CompletionsClient<reqwest::Client> to CompletionsClient<RefreshingCodexClient> with the refreshing middleware
If token refresh fails (network error, invalid refresh_token), the original request is NOT sent — the error propagates up to the caller
The RefreshingCodexClient strips any existing Authorization header from the original rig request before injecting the Bearer token (rig sets a dummy key)

RefreshingCodexClient holds token state in Arc<tokio::sync::RwLock<TokenState>> (NOT std::sync::RwLock) for thread-safe interior mutability — tokio RwLock required because refresh_access_token_at() is async and guards must be held across .await points

Concurrent refresh uses double-check locking: read lock → check expired → drop read → write lock → RE-CHECK expired → refresh only if still expired. This prevents redundant refresh calls when multiple requests detect expiry simultaneously
If TokenRefreshResponse.expires_in is None, default to 3600 seconds (1 hour) — standard OAuth 2.0 convention. The 30-second expiry buffer still applies

RefreshingCodexClient is used for ALL CodexProvider modes (not just OAuth). In API key mode, it operates in pass-through mode (no refresh, no URL rewrite, forwards to reqwest unchanged). This gives one consistent type: CompletionModel<RefreshingCodexClient>

PROV-017.description:
Add Codex OAuth login options to the ProviderSettingsScreen in the TUI.

OpenCode's pattern (dialog-connect-provider.tsx):
1. User selects a provider → sees list of auth methods (API key, 'ChatGPT Pro/Plus (browser)', 'ChatGPT Pro/Plus (headless)')
2. For OAuth browser: UI shows spinner → calls authorize endpoint → opens browser → shows 'waiting' with spinner → callback completes → success toast
3. For OAuth headless: UI shows spinner → calls authorize endpoint → displays user_code + URL → shows 'waiting' with spinner → polling completes → success toast
4. For API key: shows text input → user pastes key → submit

Codelet's ProviderSettingsScreen (src/tui/components/ProviderSettingsScreen.tsx) currently only supports API key entry and profile-based config. It needs:
1. A new 'Login with ChatGPT' option for the codex provider when no OAuth tokens exist
2. Browser login flow: calls NAPI codex_oauth_browser_login() → shows URL + spinner → waits for callback
3. Device login flow: calls NAPI codex_oauth_device_login() → shows user_code + URL → waits for polling
4. On success: refreshes provider list, sets codex as active provider
5. On failure: shows error message, allows retry

Depends on PROV-015 (NAPI bindings).

User selects 'Login with ChatGPT (browser)': screen shows spinner with 'Waiting for authorization...' text, browser opens to auth URL, user authorizes in browser, callback completes, screen shows '✓ Connected to ChatGPT' success message, provider list refreshes showing codex as configured

User selects 'Login with ChatGPT (browser)' on error screen (retry): flow restarts from scratch, new spinner shown, new browser tab opens

Selecting 'Login with ChatGPT (browser)' calls codex_oauth_browser_login() NAPI binding, shows a spinner with 'Waiting for authorization...', and resolves when the browser callback completes

On OAuth failure (timeout, network error, user cancel), an error message is shown with the option to retry or go back to the provider list
Pressing Escape during an OAuth waiting state cancels the flow and returns to the provider list

PROV-019.description:
The Codex OAuth integration (PROV-011 through PROV-018) has three critical bugs that make it unusable end-to-end:

1. **401 token_expired on every request** — When CodexProvider::new() loads tokens from ~/.codex/auth.json, it passes `expires_in: None` to RefreshingCodexClient::new_oauth(), which defaults to `Instant::now() + 3600s`. This means the client thinks tokens loaded from disk are fresh for another hour, even though they may be weeks old and already expired. The first API call fails with 401 Unauthorized (code: token_expired). The RefreshingCodexClient never gets a chance to refresh because it believes the token is still valid.

2. **Provider Settings shows 'Edit API Key' for Codex** — Pressing 'e' on the Codex (ChatGPT) provider in the /provider screen shows a generic API key editor form ('Edit API Key: Codex (ChatGPT)' with an API Key text field). Codex uses OAuth, not API keys. The 'e' key handler should either launch the OAuth flow or show a message that Codex uses OAuth authentication.

3. **Provider Settings shows wrong status for Codex** — When Codex is expanded in /provider screen, it doesn't consistently show OAuth login options or proper OAuth status indicators. The provider appears without clear indication of whether OAuth tokens exist.

examples.text: CodexProvider loads week-old tokens from auth.json, passes Some(0) to RefreshingCodexClient, first API call triggers refresh, gets 200 OK
User presses 'e' on Codex provider row — browser OAuth flow starts, not API key editor form
User presses 'e' on Anthropic provider row — API key editor form shows as usual
Codex with valid OAuth tokens shows '✓ OAuth [ChatGPT]' on the collapsed provider row
User presses 'd' on Codex provider with OAuth tokens — tokens are cleared and provider shows '(not configured)'

rules.text: Tokens loaded from disk must trigger immediate refresh — expires_in=0 forces refresh on first API call
Pressing 'e' on Codex provider must launch OAuth flow, never show API key editor
Pressing 'd' on Codex provider with OAuth tokens must disconnect OAuth (not delete API key)
Codex provider with OAuth tokens must show '✓ OAuth [ChatGPT]' status, not '(not configured)'
Non-OAuth providers (e.g., Anthropic, OpenAI) must still show API key editor on 'e' press

Key structural difference from Codex OAuth: Anthropic token endpoint uses JSON body (Content-Type: application/json) not form-encoded. Also no id_token in response — just access_token, refresh_token, expires_in. No JWT account_id extraction needed.

PKCE code can be shared between codex_oauth.rs and claude_oauth.rs — the generate_pkce() and generate_state() functions are identical. Consider extracting to a shared oauth_common module, or just re-implement (they're small).

PROV-020.description: Parent child: implement Anthropic/Claude subscription OAuth core modeled after /tmp/opencode and Codex PROV patterns.

examples.text: PKCE generated with S256: verifier is 43-char random string, challenge is Base64URL(SHA-256(verifier)), authorize URL built with code=true, client_id, response_type=code, redirect_uri, scope, code_challenge, code_challenge_method=S256, state=verifier

User pastes 'l0pnTslN...#FgE6g_6k...' — exchange fn splits on '#', sends JSON POST with code=l0pnTslN..., state=FgE6g_6k..., grant_type=authorization_code, client_id, redirect_uri, code_verifier to token endpoint, receives {access_token, refresh_token, expires_in}

Token expired: refresh_access_token sends JSON POST with grant_type=refresh_token, refresh_token, client_id to https://console.anthropic.com/v1/oauth/token, receives new {access_token, refresh_token, expires_in}

Build OAuth headers: sets Authorization=Bearer {token}, anthropic-beta merges required [oauth-2025-04-20, interleaved-thinking-2025-05-14] with any existing beta headers, sets user-agent=claude-cli/2.1.3 (external, cli), removes x-api-key
Tool name prefixing: 'Bash' → 'mcp_Bash' in tool definitions and tool_use content blocks. Response stream 'mcp_Bash' → 'Bash' in tool_result names.
URL rewriting for OAuth: https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages → https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages?beta=true
Code exchange fails (invalid code): token endpoint returns non-200, exchange fn returns error with status and body

Authorize URL for 'max' mode: https://claude.ai/oauth/authorize?code=true&client_id=9d1c250a-...&response_type=code&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fconsole.anthropic.com%2Foauth%2Fcode%2Fcallback&scope=org%3Acreate_api_key+user%3Aprofile+user%3Ainference&code_challenge=...&code_challenge_method=S256&state=...

rules.text: Anthropic OAuth uses PKCE (RFC 7636, S256) — CLIENT_ID: 9d1c250a-e61b-44d9-88ed-5944d1962f5e, authorize URL for Max mode: https://claude.ai/oauth/authorize
Token endpoint is https://console.anthropic.com/v1/oauth/token — accepts JSON body (NOT form-encoded like Codex/OpenAI)
Redirect URI is https://console.anthropic.com/oauth/code/callback — Anthropic hosts the callback page, NOT a local server. User copies authorization code from redirect page.
OAuth scope: org:create_api_key user:profile user:inference
Authorization code format is 'code#state' — the auth server returns code and state concatenated with '#' separator. The exchange function must parse this.
Token exchange request body is JSON with: code, state, grant_type=authorization_code, client_id, redirect_uri, code_verifier
Token refresh uses JSON POST to token endpoint with: grant_type=refresh_token, refresh_token, client_id

OAuth API requests require: Authorization: Bearer {access_token}, anthropic-beta header with oauth-2025-04-20 and interleaved-thinking-2025-05-14, user-agent: claude-cli/2.1.3 (external, cli), x-api-key header removed
Tool names must be prefixed with 'mcp_' when using OAuth mode — tool_use blocks in messages and tool definitions both need this prefix. Responses must strip the prefix.
The /v1/messages URL must have ?beta=true query parameter appended when using OAuth mode
State parameter in the authorize URL is set to the PKCE verifier (not a separate random value like Codex) — this simplifies CSRF validation since state == verifier
Token response contains: access_token, refresh_token, expires_in (seconds). The expires timestamp is calculated as Date.now() + expires_in * 1000.

examples.text: Happy path: browser_oauth_login() called → PKCE generated → browser opens to claude.ai/oauth/authorize → local server starts showing form → user authorizes on claude.ai → copies code#state from Anthropic callback page → pastes into form → state validated against PKCE verifier → code exchanged for tokens via JSON POST → tokens persisted to claude_auth.json → server shuts down → returns ClaudeTokens

State mismatch: user pastes code#wrongstate → parse_authorization_code extracts state → state != verifier → server returns HTML error page with CSRF warning → no tokens persisted → server shuts down → returns CSRF error
Timeout: user opens browser but never pastes code → 5 minutes elapse → server shuts down cleanly → returns timeout error
Token exchange fails: user pastes valid code#state → state validates → exchange POST to console.anthropic.com/v1/oauth/token returns 400 → server shows error page → returns exchange error
Cancel via route: user navigates to local server /cancel → server returns cancel page → shuts down → returns cancellation error

Browser fails to open: open crate fails (headless environment) → logs warning with authorize URL → local server still shows form with clickable link → user can manually navigate → flow continues normally

Server has a configurable timeout (5 minutes default) — if no code submitted, server shuts down and login fails gracefully
After successful exchange, tokens persisted to ~/.config/codelet/claude_auth.json (analogous to Codex auth.json) with access_token, refresh_token, and expires timestamp

Uses existing PROV-020 functions: generate_pkce(), build_authorize_url(), parse_authorization_code(), exchange_authorization_code(), calculate_expiry() — no duplication
Local server form page displays the authorize URL as a clickable link (fallback for environments where open crate fails)

PROV-022.description: Child of PROV-012: device code initiation, polling lifecycle, and completion/error handling for Claude subscription auth.

examples.text: Happy path: claude_headless_login() called → PKCE generated → callback invoked with authorize URL → user returns 'authcode123#verifier456' → parse_authorization_code splits on # → state matches verifier → exchange_authorization_code sends JSON POST → tokens returned → calculate_expiry computes timestamp → write_claude_auth persists to claude_auth.json → returns ClaudeAuthJson
State mismatch: user pastes 'code#wrong_state' → parse_authorization_code extracts state → state != PKCE verifier → returns CSRF mismatch error → no tokens persisted
Missing state: user pastes code without # separator → parse_authorization_code returns (code, None) → treated as missing state → error returned
Timeout: callback blocks indefinitely (user never pastes code) → timeout_ms expires → flow terminates with timeout error → no tokens persisted
Token exchange fails: user pastes valid code#state → state validates → exchange POST returns 400 → returns exchange error → no tokens persisted
Callback returns empty string: user submits empty code → error before any state validation or exchange → descriptive error

Output matches browser OAuth: headless login returns same ClaudeAuthJson struct as claude_browser_oauth_login (PROV-021) — access_token, refresh_token, expires — both flows are interchangeable for downstream consumers

rules.text: Anthropic has NO RFC 8628 device authorization endpoints — headless auth is a CLI code-paste flow: display authorize URL, user visits on another device, copies code#state from Anthropic callback page, enters it via callback/stdin
Headless login generates PKCE + builds authorize URL using existing PROV-020 functions (generate_pkce, build_authorize_url), then displays the URL for the user to visit on another device

Code entry is via an async callback function (not stdin directly) — the callback receives the authorize URL and returns the user-pasted code#state string. This allows NAPI/TUI callers (PROV-024/PROV-025) to provide their own input mechanism
State validation: the state portion of the pasted code#state must match the PKCE verifier. Mismatch is a CSRF error (same as PROV-021 rule). Missing state (no # separator) is also an error.

Token exchange uses existing PROV-020 exchange_authorization_code() with the configurable base URL (production: console.anthropic.com, tests: wiremock). JSON POST with code, state, grant_type, client_id, redirect_uri, code_verifier.

Headless login has a configurable timeout — if the callback does not return within the timeout, the flow terminates gracefully with a timeout error

No HTTP server, no browser opening, no port binding — headless login is purely an async function that generates PKCE, invokes the code-entry callback, validates, exchanges, and persists. Much simpler than PROV-021.

architectureNotes.text: New file: codelet/providers/src/claude_refreshing_client.rs — Implements RefreshingClaudeClient struct that wraps reqwest::Client and implements rig's HttpClientExt trait. Contains ClaudeTokenState struct with access_token, refresh_token, token_endpoint_base, and expires_at (Instant). Arc<tokio::sync::RwLock<ClaudeTokenState>> for shared mutable state. ClaudeTokenMode enum: OAuth{token_state} and ApiKey. ~200 lines, mirrors codex/refreshing_client.rs structure.

Key structural difference from Codex RefreshingClient: Claude's RefreshingClaudeClient is SIMPLER — no URL rewriting needed (rig AnthropicExt::build_uri does ?beta=true), no extra headers like ChatGPT-Account-Id or originator. Only handles Authorization: Bearer header replacement and token refresh. Static headers (anthropic-beta, anthropic-version, user-agent, x-app) remain set at rig client build time.

ClaudeProvider modification: claude.rs struct fields change from CompletionModel (defaulting to reqwest::Client) to CompletionModel<RefreshingClaudeClient> and from Client to Client<RefreshingClaudeClient>. from_api_key_with_mode_and_model() constructs RefreshingClaudeClient and passes via .http_client() to rig anthropic::ClientBuilder. OAuth mode: new_oauth(), API key mode: new_api_key(). Agent builder's client() type changes correspondingly.

Token persistence uses async write_claude_auth() from claude_auth.rs (PROV-021). Since HttpClientExt methods return non-async futures (impl Future), persistence is spawned as a fire-and-forget tokio::spawn task — same pattern as codex refreshing_client.rs persist_tokens() using std::thread::spawn for synchronous write_codex_auth(). For Claude, write_claude_auth is async so we use tokio::spawn directly.

assumptions: This card does NOT implement: tool name prefixing/stripping (mcp_ prefix — tracked as part of the request body transformation which may be handled at a higher layer or in a future card), NAPI bindings (PROV-024), TUI integration (PROV-025), or model routing (PROV-026). Purely the HTTP middleware layer for token refresh and auth header injection.

Reuses from PROV-020 (claude_oauth.rs): refresh_access_token_at(), ClaudeTokenResponse. Reuses from PROV-021 (claude_auth.rs): write_claude_auth(), ClaudeAuthJson, calculate_expiry(). No new crate dependencies.
PROV-023.description: Child of PROV-012: refresh-on-expiry behavior, persistence updates, and auth failure state transitions.

examples.text: Happy path (valid token): ClaudeProvider makes API call → RefreshingClaudeClient reads token state → token has 30min remaining → skips refresh → strips any existing Authorization header → injects Authorization: Bearer {access_token} → forwards to reqwest → response returned

Token expired mid-session: ClaudeProvider makes API call → RefreshingClaudeClient detects token expired → calls claude_oauth::refresh_access_token_at() with stored refresh_token → gets new ClaudeTokenResponse → updates in-memory state → persists to claude_auth.json (best-effort) → injects fresh Bearer token → forwards request → response returned

Token refresh fails (invalid refresh_token): RefreshingClaudeClient detects expiry → calls refresh_access_token_at() → gets 401 → returns rig::http_client::Error → original API request NOT sent → user sees auth error
Streaming request with expired token: RefreshingClaudeClient refreshes token via send_streaming() path → fresh Bearer injected → SSE stream returned with fresh credentials

API key mode pass-through: ClaudeProvider::from_api_key_with_mode_and_model() creates RefreshingClaudeClient in ApiKey mode → requests flow through to reqwest unchanged — no token refresh, no header modification, rig's static headers preserved
Token within expiry buffer: token expires in 20 seconds, buffer is 30 seconds → now + 30s >= expires_at → proactive refresh triggered → request uses refreshed token

Concurrent requests during refresh: two requests arrive while token is expired → first acquires write lock → refreshes → second finds fresh token on re-check → both proceed with same refreshed token → only one HTTP refresh call made

Tokens loaded from disk: OAuth tokens exist in claude_auth.json from previous session → ClaudeProvider passes Some(0) for expires_in_secs → token immediately expired → first API request triggers refresh before sending

ClaudeProvider integration: from_api_key_with_mode_and_model() in OAuth mode creates RefreshingClaudeClient with initial tokens → passes as .http_client() to rig anthropic::ClientBuilder → rig client type becomes Client<RefreshingClaudeClient> → CompletionModel<RefreshingClaudeClient> → provider methods use it transparently

rules.text: Implement HttpClientExt trait for RefreshingClaudeClient that wraps reqwest::Client, intercepting every HTTP request in OAuth mode to check token expiry, refresh if needed, and inject the current Authorization: Bearer header
Token expiry tracked using tokio::time::Instant with a 30-second buffer — if now + 30s >= expires_at, token is considered expired and must be refreshed before the request
Token refresh uses existing refresh_access_token_at() from claude_oauth.rs (PROV-020) with configurable base URL for testability (production: console.anthropic.com, tests: wiremock)
After refresh, updated tokens persisted to claude_auth.json via write_claude_auth() from claude_auth.rs (PROV-021) — persistence is best-effort (errors logged, don't fail the request)
RefreshingClaudeClient strips any existing Authorization header from the rig request and injects Authorization: Bearer {current_access_token} — rig's static headers may contain a stale token

RefreshingClaudeClient holds token state in Arc<tokio::sync::RwLock<ClaudeTokenState>> for thread-safe interior mutability — tokio RwLock required because refresh is async and guards must be held across .await points

Concurrent refresh uses double-check locking: read lock → check expired → drop read → write lock → RE-CHECK expired → refresh only if still expired. Prevents redundant refresh calls when multiple requests detect expiry simultaneously
If token refresh fails (network error, invalid refresh_token), the original request is NOT sent — the error propagates up to the caller as rig::http_client::Error

RefreshingClaudeClient is used for ALL ClaudeProvider modes (not just OAuth). In API key mode, it operates in pass-through mode (no refresh, no header injection, forwards to reqwest unchanged). This gives one consistent type: CompletionModel<RefreshingClaudeClient>

URL rewriting (?beta=true) is NOT done by RefreshingClaudeClient — the rig AnthropicExt::build_uri() already handles this via AnthropicKey::is_oauth_token() detection. RefreshingClaudeClient only handles auth headers and token refresh
Static headers (anthropic-beta, anthropic-version, user-agent, x-app) remain set at rig client build time and are NOT modified by RefreshingClaudeClient — only Authorization changes dynamically

ClaudeProvider struct fields become CompletionModel<RefreshingClaudeClient> and Client<RefreshingClaudeClient> (anthropic::Client parameterized with custom HTTP backend). ClaudeProvider::from_api_key_with_mode_and_model() constructs the RefreshingClaudeClient and passes it via .http_client()
Tokens loaded from disk (via read_claude_auth from PROV-021) should use Some(0) for expires_in_secs to force immediate refresh on first API request — the persisted token may be expired

architectureNotes.text: New file: codelet/napi/src/claude_oauth.rs — All NAPI functions in one module. Imports claude_browser_oauth_login from claude_oauth_server, generate_pkce/build_authorize_url/parse_authorization_code/exchange_authorization_code/calculate_expiry from claude_oauth, refresh_access_token_at from claude_oauth, read_claude_auth/write_claude_auth/get_claude_auth_path from claude_auth. Mirrors codex_oauth.rs structure.

NapiClaudeTokens #[napi(object)] struct maps to ClaudeAuthJson with access_token, refresh_token, expires (f64 for JS compatibility). NapiClaudeHeadlessStartResult #[napi(object)] with authorize_url (String) and pkce_verifier (String) — verifier returned to TS so it can be passed back to complete().
lib.rs registration: add `mod claude_oauth;` under #[cfg(not(feature = "noop"))] and `pub use claude_oauth::*;` — same pattern as codex_oauth module.

Headless two-phase approach: claude_oauth_headless_start() generates PKCE via generate_pkce(), builds authorize URL via build_authorize_url(), returns NapiClaudeHeadlessStartResult. claude_oauth_headless_complete(code_with_state, pkce_verifier) parses code#state, validates state == pkce_verifier, exchanges via exchange_authorization_code(), persists via write_claude_auth(), returns NapiClaudeTokens. No CodeEntryFn callback needed — NAPI boundary stays clean.

Key difference from Codex NAPI (PROV-015): Claude auth is simpler — no id_token, no account_id, no JWT extraction. But claude_auth is async (tokio::fs) so get_tokens and clear_tokens are async NAPI functions (vs sync in Codex). Also no device polling — headless is start+complete instead of start+poll.

assumptions: This card does NOT implement TUI integration (PROV-025), provider routing (PROV-026), or parity testing (PROV-027). Purely the NAPI bridge between Rust OAuth code and TypeScript.
All Rust OAuth modules (claude_oauth.rs, claude_oauth_server.rs, claude_headless_login.rs, claude_auth.rs, claude_refreshing_client.rs) are already implemented and tested by PROV-020/021/022/023.

examples.text: TUI calls claude_oauth_browser_login(): tokio spawns claude_browser_oauth_login(), local server starts, browser opens, user authorizes on claude.ai, pastes code#state, tokens exchanged, Promise resolves with NapiClaudeTokens containing access_token, refresh_token, expires

TUI calls claude_oauth_headless_start(): generates PKCE, builds authorize URL, returns NapiClaudeHeadlessStartResult with authorize_url and pkce_verifier. TUI displays URL. User visits URL, authorizes, copies code#state.

TUI calls claude_oauth_headless_complete('authcode123#verifier456', 'verifier456'): validates state matches pkce_verifier, exchanges code via JSON POST, persists tokens to claude_auth.json, returns NapiClaudeTokens
Headless complete with wrong state: claude_oauth_headless_complete('code#wrong_state', 'real_verifier') → Promise rejects with error containing 'CSRF validation failed — state mismatch'
Headless complete with no hash separator: claude_oauth_headless_complete('codeonly', 'verifier') → Promise rejects with error containing 'Missing state'
TUI calls claude_oauth_refresh_token('rt_abc123'): Rust calls refresh_access_token_at(), returns NapiClaudeTokens with refreshed access_token. Persists updated tokens to claude_auth.json.
Token refresh fails: claude_oauth_refresh_token('invalid_rt') → Promise rejects with error describing the failure status
TUI calls claude_oauth_get_tokens() with valid claude_auth.json: returns NapiClaudeTokens with access_token, refresh_token, expires populated
TUI calls claude_oauth_get_tokens() with no claude_auth.json: returns null (not an error — absence of tokens is a valid state)
Browser login times out: claude_oauth_browser_login() Promise rejects with error containing 'timed out'
TUI calls claude_oauth_clear_tokens() with existing claude_auth.json: file deleted, subsequent get_tokens returns null
TUI calls claude_oauth_clear_tokens() with no claude_auth.json: returns Ok(()) — idempotent, not an error

rules.text: claude_oauth_browser_login() is an async NAPI function that spawns a tokio task to run claude_browser_oauth_login() from claude_oauth_server.rs, returning a Promise<NapiClaudeTokens> to TypeScript

Headless login uses a two-phase design: claude_oauth_headless_start() returns NapiClaudeHeadlessStartResult with authorize_url and pkce_verifier (so TUI can display URL and collect code), then claude_oauth_headless_complete(code_with_state, pkce_verifier) validates state, exchanges code, and returns NapiClaudeTokens

claude_oauth_refresh_token(refresh_token: string) is an async NAPI function that calls refresh_access_token_at() from claude_oauth.rs and returns NapiClaudeTokens with refreshed tokens persisted to claude_auth.json

claude_oauth_get_tokens() is an async NAPI function that reads claude_auth.json via read_claude_auth() and returns NapiClaudeTokens or null — async because claude_auth uses tokio::fs unlike Codex which is sync
claude_oauth_clear_tokens() is an async NAPI function that deletes claude_auth.json (or clears its content) for disconnect — mirrors codex_oauth_clear_tokens() pattern
All NAPI functions convert Rust errors to napi::Error via Error::from_reason() — TypeScript sees rejected promises with descriptive error messages
NapiClaudeTokens is an #[napi(object)] struct with fields: access_token (String), refresh_token (String), expires (f64, milliseconds since epoch) — maps to ClaudeAuthJson from claude_auth.rs
The NAPI module file is codelet/napi/src/claude_oauth.rs, registered in lib.rs under #[cfg(not(feature = "noop"))] — same pattern as codex_oauth module

PROV-028.description:
Multiple critical and medium-severity issues found via visual testing of the OAuth TUI integration for both Anthropic (PROV-012) and Codex (PROV-011).

### 🔴 Critical Issues

**1. Claude browser OAuth opens wrong URL — code entry form never shown (PROV-021/PROV-025)**

The "Login with Claude (browser)" flow is completely broken. `claude_oauth_server.rs` line 118 calls `open::that(&auth_url)` which opens the Anthropic authorization URL directly in the browser. After the user authorizes, they land on `platform.claude.com/oauth/code/callback` with a code to paste, but the local form page at `http://localhost:{port}/` — which has the actual paste input — was never opened in the browser. The TUI only shows "Waiting for authorization..." with no code input. The flow is dead.

Fix: Change `open::that(&auth_url)` to `open::that(format!("http://localhost:{port}/"))` — the form page already links to the auth URL via `target="_blank"`.

**2. Expanded Codex provider shows zero sub-items (PROV-017)**

When Codex has OAuth tokens and is expanded, `buildNavItems()` in `useProviderSettingsState.ts` pushes zero items: login options are guarded by `!provider.hasOAuthTokens`, profiles array is empty (OAuth providers don't use profiles), and "Create Profile" is guarded by `!isOAuthProvider()`. Result: completely empty expansion.

### 🟡 Medium Issues

**3. Codex status indicator disappears when expanded**

Collapsed: `▶ Codex (ChatGPT) ✓ OAuth [ChatGPT]`. Expanded: `▼ Codex (ChatGPT)` — status text gone. Likely a `wrap="truncate"` issue or selection highlighting problem.

**4. Headless code input renders as single unwrapped line**

When pasting the authorization code into the headless code entry field, the text has no width constraint or wrapping. OAuth codes are 80-200+ chars and push the layout down off screen. The `<Text>{mode.codeInput}</Text>` element in `ProviderSettingsPanel.tsx:403-408` needs a width-constrained Box or truncation.

**5. Authorize URL not copyable — no keybind, not a terminal hyperlink**

The headless screen shows the auth URL (~300-400 chars) as plain blue text. Users can't select it, copy it, or click it. No keybind exists in `oauthModeHandler.ts` to copy to clipboard. Without a way to access the URL, headless mode is also functionally broken. Need at minimum a `c` keybind to copy, ideally also render as an OSC 8 terminal hyperlink.

**6. PROV-012 parent stuck in "specifying" — all 8 children done**

PROV-020 through PROV-027 are all done but PROV-012 remains in specifying. Also has no Example Mapping, no estimate, no linked features.

**7. PROV-011 parent stuck in "specifying" — all 5 children done**

PROV-013 through PROV-017 are all done but PROV-011 remains in specifying.

**8. Previous review-fixes.md on PROV-012 never applied**

Parallel test failures (#[serial] annotations), user-agent version spec drift, mcp_ prefixing scope clarification.

### 🔵 Design: Browser + Headless Should Be One Flow

Since Anthropic's redirect URI is remote (not localhost), BOTH flows require manual code pasting. The browser/headless distinction should be merged into a single "Login with Claude" that auto-opens browser AND shows the URL + code entry in the TUI simultaneously. This eliminates the confusing choice and the need for the local HTTP form server. **This should be a follow-up card.**

### Screenshots

See attached wrong1.png through wrong4.png and the comprehensive analysis in oauth-tui-bugs-analysis.md.

PROV-029.description:
The Anthropic provider, which is an OAuth provider (authType: 'oauth'), is displaying a profile row '📁 anthropic → http://localhost:8888' and a header count '(1 profile)' when expanded in the Provider Settings TUI.

This is wrong on multiple levels:

1. **Profiles are conceptually wrong for OAuth providers.** Profiles exist for local server configurations (vLLM, Ollama custom endpoints) where you need a baseUrl + apiKey pair. OAuth providers authenticate via OAuth tokens, not API keys pointed at custom endpoints.

2. **Stale profile in config.** The user config `~/.fspec/fspec-config.json` has a profile under `providers.anthropic.profiles.anthropic` containing `baseUrl: http://localhost:8888` and what appears to be an OAuth access token (`sk-ant-oat01-*`) stored as an apiKey. The `localhost:8888` URL is the local OAuth form server — this profile was likely created accidentally during OAuth development/testing.

3. **Missing display guard.** `buildNavItems()` in `useProviderSettingsState.ts` iterates `provider.profiles` (lines 187-193) without checking if the provider is an OAuth provider. The 'Create Profile' button IS correctly guarded (line 195), but existing profiles still render.

4. **Missing load guard.** `reload()` (line 304) calls `loadProviderProfiles(providerId)` for ALL providers, including OAuth ones. It should skip loading profiles for OAuth providers.

5. **Missing creation guard.** `saveProfile()` in `provider-config.ts` accepts any providerId — there's no validation to reject profile creation for OAuth providers.

6. **Missing header guard.** The '(N profiles)' count in `ProviderSettingsPanel.tsx` (line 518-524) renders whenever `profileCount > 0` without checking isOAuthProvider.

See attached analysis and screenshot.

PROV-033.description:
The extractCodexSection() logic in modelInitializationService.ts uses isCodexModel() which checks modelId.toLowerCase().includes('codex'). This is fundamentally wrong.

The models.dev OpenAI provider returns models like gpt-5.2-chat-latest, gpt-5.2-pro, gpt-5.2, gpt-5.1, gpt-5-pro, gpt-5-nano, gpt-5-mini, gpt-5, o3-pro, o4-mini, o3, gpt-4.1, gpt-4.1-nano, gpt-4.1-mini, o1-pro, o3-mini, o1, gpt-4o-2024-11-20 — NONE of which contain 'codex' in their ID.

- 'OpenAI' section with 19+ cloud models (gpt-5.2, o3-pro, etc.) — WRONG
- 'Codex (ChatGPT)' section with only 8 models — WRONG

When Codex OAuth tokens exist, ALL models from the OpenAI provider on models.dev are accessed via Codex OAuth. They should ALL go into the 'Codex (ChatGPT)' section. The 'OpenAI' cloud section should not exist at all when Codex OAuth is active.

The label 'OpenAI' / 'OpenAI API' is reserved for local model profiles (vLLM, Ollama, etc.) which already display correctly as 'openai: profilename' with 📁 folder icons.

The test fixtures in codexModelInitialization.test.ts are also wrong — they use fake model IDs like 'gpt-5.3-codex' and 'gpt-5.2-codex' which don't exist on models.dev. The tests pass but test the wrong thing.

PROV-034.description:
When Codex OAuth is active, models.dev returns the full OpenAI provider catalog (gpt-5.2, gpt-5, o3-pro, o4-mini, gpt-4.1, o1, gpt-5-mini, gpt-5-nano, etc.). However, the Codex CLI subscription only has access to a specific subset of Codex-specific models.

Analysis of the openai/codex repository (codex-rs/core/models.json) reveals that Codex subscriptions only support 12 models:
- gpt-5.3-codex (not available on free plan)
- gpt-5.2-codex
- gpt-5.1-codex-max
- gpt-5.1-codex (hidden)
- gpt-5.2 (visible)
- gpt-5.1 (hidden)
- gpt-5-codex (hidden)
- gpt-5 (hidden)
- gpt-oss-120b (hidden)
- gpt-oss-20b (hidden)
- gpt-5.1-codex-mini
- gpt-5-codex-mini (hidden)

Models NOT available through Codex subscriptions include:
- All reasoning models: o3, o3-pro, o4-mini, o1, o1-pro, o3-mini
- Older GPT variants: gpt-4.1, gpt-4.1-mini, gpt-4.1-nano, gpt-4o
- Size variants: gpt-5-mini, gpt-5-nano, gpt-5-pro

Currently the model selector shows ALL models from models.dev in the Codex (ChatGPT) section, letting users select models that will fail at runtime. We need dynamic filtering that cross-references the models.dev catalog against the Codex-supported model list.

The Codex CLI fetches its model list dynamically from a /models endpoint (with the bundled models.json as fallback). The server filters by plan type and client version. Our filtering should ideally match this behavior rather than hardcoding the model list.

Key insight: The 'available_in_plans' field exists in models.json but is NOT consumed by the Rust client — filtering happens server-side. The 'supported_in_api' and 'visibility' fields control client-side display. All 12 bundled models have supported_in_api=true, and only 4 have visibility='list' (shown in picker).

examples.text: User has Codex OAuth active. models.dev returns 19 OpenAI models including o3-pro, gpt-4.1, gpt-5-mini. Model selector shows only 5 picker-visible Codex models: gpt-5.3-codex, gpt-5.2-codex, gpt-5.1-codex-max, gpt-5.2, gpt-5.1-codex-mini. The 14 unsupported models are not shown.

User has NO Codex OAuth but HAS an OpenAI API key. models.dev returns 19 models. All 19 models are shown in the OpenAI section because API key users can access any model from the OpenAI platform — no Codex filtering applied.

OpenAI releases a new model 'gpt-6-codex' and adds it to the Codex /models endpoint. Without a code release, the allowlist config is updated to include gpt-6-codex, and the model appears in the selector on next startup.

rules.text: When Codex OAuth is active, the model selector must only display models that exist in the Codex-supported catalog — not the full models.dev OpenAI provider list. Models like o3-pro, o4-mini, gpt-4.1, gpt-5-mini, gpt-5-nano etc. must be filtered out.

The Codex model allowlist must NOT be hardcoded — it should be derived from a maintainable data source (e.g. a JSON config file or a fetched endpoint) so it can be updated as OpenAI adds/removes models from the Codex catalog without code changes.

Filtering must use slug prefix matching (like the Codex CLI does) — e.g. a Codex catalog entry 'gpt-5.2-codex' should match models.dev entries like 'gpt-5.2-codex-2026-03-01'. Exact match alone is insufficient.
When no Codex OAuth is active (API key only), the full models.dev catalog must be shown unfiltered — the Codex allowlist only applies when Codex subscription auth is in use.
Local model profiles (openai: profilename with 📁 icon) must NOT be filtered — only cloud models from the OpenAI provider on models.dev are subject to Codex allowlist filtering.

PROV-037.description: GPT-5.3 Codex stops after producing brief commentary text (33 output tokens, 0 reasoning tokens) without ever calling tools. The root cause is that our Codex provider does not send the `reasoning` parameter in Responses API requests. Three bugs: (1) `_thinking_config` parameter in create_rig_agent is completely ignored (underscore prefix), (2) get_thinking_config() has no branch for codex/openai providers and returns empty {}, (3) the request body is missing reasoning, tool_choice, include, and parallel_tool_calls fields that codex-rs always sends. Without reasoning enabled, the model cannot perform multi-step agentic reasoning and tool use.

get_thinking_config('gpt-5.3-codex', Medium) returns {reasoning: {effort: 'medium', summary: 'auto'}}
create_rig_agent with None thinking_config still sends default reasoning: {effort: 'high', summary: 'auto'} for Codex models
Wire request JSON includes reasoning, include, tool_choice, and parallel_tool_calls matching codex-rs format

get_thinking_config() must return OpenAI Responses API reasoning format ({reasoning: {effort, summary}}) for codex and openai reasoning providers
Responses API request must include reasoning.effort (high default), reasoning.summary (auto), include: [reasoning.encrypted_content], and tool_choice: auto
complete_with_tools must also inject reasoning config into additional_params, not just create_rig_agent
Default reasoning config must be applied when no thinking_config is provided (Codex models always need reasoning)

PROV-038.description: The Codex provider (using OpenAI Responses API via rig-core) never receives token usage data during streaming. The TUI displays 'tokens: 0↓ 130↑ [0%]' — input tokens stuck at 0 and context fill percentage always at 0%. Output tokens are estimated from chunk lengths but input tokens are never populated. Root cause: the rig-core Responses API streaming implementation never yields RawStreamingChoice::Usage events, unlike the Chat Completions API and Anthropic providers which do.
